notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0244d.stoa005.opp-l: pr.2: the passage ends with scribal rubrics (incipit/explicit) from several manuscripts; stray letters (B, P, v) are apparently manuscript sigla and are omitted. 'lnlustnus' read as 'inlustrius', 'purus' as 'purius'. 1.1: 'desejto' read as 'deserto'. 1.5: the construction 'ne nautae quidem probabili' is elliptical; '[it is not strange]' supplied from the preceding clause.

In 1.6 'tnmultuosis' read as 'tumultuosis'. In 1.9 'uelut alioqui greges' is odd; translated as if 'uelut adloqui greges' ('to sing and as it were address the flocks'), rendered loosely as 'to sing to the flocks, as it were'. In 1.11 'praeruptae rupis' rendered 'precipitous rock'.

In 20 the punctuation of the edition ('cum propriis uitiis et passionibus: rationes...'; 'more surdae aspidis.') has been taken as running on into the following clauses. 'innitis' (15) read as 'inuitis'; 'uon' (14) as 'non'; 'sine' (18) as 'siue'; 'fiagitium' (20) as 'flagitium'. In 14, 'huic qui erudiendis atque instituendis ad uirtutem populis praeest' is rendered as one who presides over peoples to be trained in virtue.

Scanning errors read as evident: 26 'uos' as 'nos'; 22 'nou' as 'non', 'doi' as 'dei'; 24 'inuifus' as 'inuitus'. In 21 the edition's full stop before 'est nobis omne certamen' seems misplaced; the clause is taken with what follows.

In §32 'intlalltur' is read as 'inflantur' (puffed up). §36 carries the edition's combined numbering '36. 37.' In §36–37 'afluentiam' is read as 'affluentiam'. In §38 the clause 'neque rursum tantum putare agere pro Christo' is somewhat compressed; it is rendered as continuing the construction 'oportet... non ita putare'.

§41: the text reads 'Mambres', the Latin form of Jambres (2 Tim. 3:8); rendered 'Jambres'. §46: 'nino' is a scanning error for 'uino'. §47: the proverb (Greek 'en pithōi tēn kerameian') means learning a craft by starting on the largest piece.

Line 49: 'bosor abluant' is evidently corrupt; rendered by sense as 'wash off the filth' (perhaps for 'sordes' or similar). Line 53: 'substantialem populum' rendered 'a people of his own' (cf. Greek periousios).

55: 'per speculum et in aenigmate' rendered 'through a glass and in a riddle'. 57: 'ip specula' read as 'in specula'; 'Itabyrium' is Mount Tabor (Itabyrion). 56: 'principes Taneos' = princes of Tanis (Isa. 19:11). 59: 'curationem' (proclaim a healing) is odd; Joel has 'proclaim a service/assembly' (Greek therapeia), which Rufinus may have rendered too literally. 60: 'iudex accipit' — object (bribes) supplied. 61: 'pollntos' read as 'pollutos'. 62: 'lesum' read as 'Iesum' (Joshua the high priest); 'falcem' follows the Greek/LXX reading 'sickle' for the flying scroll (Zech. 5:1). 63: 'et super agnos uisitabo' follows the LXX 'lambs' (Hebrew 'he-goats').

Evident scanning errors corrected silently: 'si gula' = singula (67), 'deSere' = deflere (67), 'congregara' = congregare and 'past/.ibus' = pastoribus (66), 'mundan' = mundari (71), 'Ific' = hic (74). In 72 '(multo)' is an editorial supplement, rendered as [far]. In 74 'totam mentem' (Greek: the whole Mind, i.e. God) is rendered 'the whole Mind'.

§93: 'miserum me' makes no sense in context and appears corrupt (perhaps for something like 'nam' or 'nimirum'); it is marked [...] and left untranslated. §87: 'the beast' is presumably the persecuting emperor (Valens in Rufinus's framing, Julian in Gregory's original). §88 'mentem' in the following stretch and similar small scan errors ('aocios', 'nemocoronatur') were read as evident.

102–103: 'aifectio' read as 'affectio'. 'parente ... falso' (of Jacob deceiving Isaac) is awkward and may be corrupt; rendered as 'deceiving his father'. 96: the subject of 'adaperit' is unexpressed; [the Lord] supplied. 'aporroea' is Greek aporroia, 'emanation' (cf. Wisdom 7:25).

In 117 the text after 'Amen' is a run of manuscript colophons from the edition's apparatus, each followed by its siglum (A, C, V, v); I have rendered them and kept the sigla in brackets. 'NL DNI' is the abbreviation for 'natali domini'. In 116 'iliorum' is read as 'filiorum' (sons). In 113 'derelicata' (109) is read as 'derelicta'. In 115 the run-together 'utouisadoccisionemadducebatur' is read as 'ut ouis ad occisionem adducebatur'. In 113 'in quantum' (115) is taken loosely as 'so that some'; the phrase is awkward in the Latin.

The first six lines are the edition's list of manuscript sigla, and the heading of this stretch is oration VII although the preceding line announced II; the library's sequence appears to skip here. 'MONACHOKUM' read as monachorum. Section 7.1 runs through matter that in the edition belongs to sections 1–3 (numbering 2–3 not marked). 'omni rei tempus' seems to lack a verb or more; text may be defective there. '[sacrificium deo est]' is bracketed in the edition, probably as an editorial deletion. Scanning errors corrected: nieo/labns (meo/labiis), nonum (nouum), cognonimus (cognouimus), nastantis (uastantis), estexterminn (exterminii), mtentatio (intentatio), uouissimum (nouissimum).

7.12: 'facellatione' is unintelligible as printed and probably corrupt (Amos 4:9 lists blight, mildew, and other afflictions); rendered as [...]. Obvious scanning errors read as: sustineremus (for 'sutreremus'), increpationes, intuemini, a uobis (for 'a nobis', 7.10), per (for 'lper'), aut (for 'faut'), commonitionibus, duri (for 'duii'), conprehendet, iratus. 'feruurae' (7.11) taken as burning eruptions/boils.

13: 'conpunctionem domini ... adfligimur pro nobis' is read as 'pro uobis' (afflicted for you); 'poase' read as 'posse', 'inmiuentis' as 'inminentis'. 14: 'elenemus' read as 'eleuemus', 'dementia' as 'clementia'. 17: 'pascuagre. gibus' read as 'pascua gregibus', 'mpiorum' as 'impiorum'; 'male dictum Gelboe montes ... suscipiunt' is awkward (subject unclear), taken as the lands everywhere receiving the curse of the mountains of Gilboa.

In 7.20 the line ends with editorial apparatus and manuscript explicits/incipits (e.g. 'EXPLICIT LIBER SCT GREGORII DE GRANDINIS UASTATIONE...', notes on the spurious 'de fide' and the absence of the Arian oration in some codices); these are not part of the text and have been left untranslated. Also in 7.20 the clause 'ista quae deorsum est cottidianum et nostra terra perpetuum' is awkward and possibly corrupt; rendered literally (the earthly land [giving] the daily fruit, our land the everlasting). The lines 'R = ...' to 'v = ...' are the edition's list of manuscript sigla, translated as such. 'Argentinac' read as 'Argentinae' (Strasbourg). In 9.2 'coalumna' read as 'coalumna' (fostered together, i.e. companion from birth).

Ch. 7: 'quomodo nolunt' (however they do not will) is odd beside 'quo uolunt'; translated as 'however we do not will', but 'quomodo uolunt' may be intended. Ch. 8: 'non quam potest' read as 'quam potest' ('as many as he can'). Ch. 9: 'sub die' taken as 'in a day'.

The Greek in the scanned text is garbled. "cnbioi [q;a" is taken as αὐτὸς ἔφα ("he himself said"), the Pythagorean formula. "νισωτάμωσνετεμ" is μετενσωμάτωσιν written backwards in the scan. "Chnsti" is read as Christi, and "m promptu" in the previous stretch as in promptu.

nodes.text: PREFACE OF RUFINUS TO APRONIANUS.

As I was setting out from the City, you urged me strongly, Apronianus, dearest son, to spend some work on you even while absent, so that the necessity of my departure might not keep us from our accustomed studies. You asked, then, that Gregory be turned into Latin for you, a man beyond comparison in every respect, who, famous in word and deeds, gave the churches a most brilliant light of the knowledge of Christ, since he taught what he did and did not condemn himself by acting contrary to what he taught. He came from a home in Cappadocia, born of a father who was a bishop and of a mother who was also very devout. He was brought up and educated at Athens as few have been, and yet in the life of the schools he did not yield to the allurements of his age or of his companions and betray his chastity; but, like a treasure entrusted to him by God, he brought back to a chaste home the seal of chastity unbroken. Indeed, while he was flourishing in the study of philosophy at Athens, he saw in his sleep, as he sat reading, two very beautiful women sit down on his right and on his left. Looking at them rather sternly, from the prompting of chastity, he asked who they were and what they wanted. But they, embracing him rather familiarly and eagerly, said: 'Do not take it amiss, young man; we are well known to you and familiar — for one of us is called Wisdom, the other Chastity — and we have been sent by the Lord to live with you, because you have prepared for us a pleasant and very clean dwelling in your heart.' Then afterwards, when on account of his outstanding progress in letters he was being pressed to teach oratory at Athens, he secretly boarded a ship and left. And when he had entrusted himself to the sea without having tried it, he was beset by a storm, in which he vowed that he would serve God. And while he was doing this, he was suddenly appointed to the priesthood by his father the bishop. Taking this hard, he went away for a time; but afterwards he returned and delivered this apologetic discourse in the church, setting out the reasons for his departure and also for his return. After this, on his father's death, he succeeded to the episcopate at Nazianzus, a small town. And from there, when after the times of Valens the Arian the catholics had recovered the churches, he was prevailed upon to go to Constantinople to establish and teach the church. There, while he was doing a magnificent work in the word of God and almost daily converting countless multitudes from the heretics to the true faith, envy, as usually happens, followed upon glory. But he was so perfect in the fear of God that, when he perceived that there was dispute among the bishops on his account, he at once withdrew of his own accord, saying only that prophetic word: 'If this storm is because of me, take me and throw me into the sea, and let the commotion cease from you.'

Nothing can be found more commendable and holier than his life, nor more brilliant and illustrious than his eloquence, nor purer and more correct than his faith, nor fuller and more perfect than his knowledge; he alone is the one about whose faith not even parties and factions at variance with one another, as usually happens, have been able to dispute, but he has obtained such merit with God and the churches of God that whoever dares to oppose his teaching in any point is by that very fact shown to be rather a heretic himself; for it is a manifest sign that anyone who does not agree with Gregory in faith is not of the right faith. Read him, then, without any scruple at all, knowing however that the necessity of translation dims not a little the resplendent light of his eloquence in Greek. Whether the poverty of our language or the very nature of translation does this, you, who are skilled in both tongues, will better judge. FROM THE GREEK, HAPPILY. HERE ENDS THE PROLOGUE OF GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS, BISHOP. HERE BEGINS HIS APOLOGETIC, TRANSLATED INTO LATIN FROM THE GREEK. HERE ENDS THE PROLOGUE. HERE BEGINS THE APOLOGETIC OF SAINT GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS.
I. APOLOGETIC.

1. I have been conquered, and I confess that I have been overcome; I have submitted to the Lord and have besought him. For it is fitting that blessed David should open the door of speech for me, or rather he himself who spoke in David and who even now speaks through him. For the best order is that of every word or work both the beginning should be taken by us from God and the completion referred back to God. The reason for which I went away some time ago, overcome as it were by a kind of weariness and indignation, and went far off in flight and dwelt in the desert for no short time, may perhaps seem one thing to some and another to others, to those who are held either by hatred towards me, as usually happens, or by love. And the fact that then we seemed somewhat wild and harsh, but now have grown gentle and have returned to what we were before, one blames as inconstancy, another welcomes the deed. For nothing is sweeter to people than to talk of others' affairs and to busy themselves with others' affairs, especially if it happens that some are preoccupied by hatred or by love. By these above all the truth is always hidden and stolen away. Let others, then, as I said, think different things; but I will set forth openly, without any shame, what is true, giving satisfaction to both parties, that is, both to those who are moved by affection towards us and also to those who are moved by hatred, in some things being my own accuser, but for some giving satisfaction as well.

2. And so that our discourse may proceed in order, I will first speak of my fear and former dread. For I will not allow suspicions about me to remain with any of those who examine either our good points or the opposite with curious scrutiny. For this too is a duty of religion: to tend with a satisfying word any who may perhaps seem to be wounded by the darts of suspicion, since indeed it is best of all that no one, either by sinning or by being placed under suspicion of sin, should, if it can be done and the matter allows, set a stumbling block or scandal before the brethren. For we know how severe a punishment has been laid down by the Lord for one who scandalizes one of the least.

3. I, then, O excellent and devout men, did not run into these things as one unskilled or foolish, nor — that I too may boast a little — as someone arrogant and despising divine laws and ordinances. For I know that, just as in our body some members govern the body and preside over all its movements, while others are governed and render obedience to those that govern, so also in the church God has ordained, administering it by the law of equity and, through his divine providence by which he orders all things, apportioning the privileges of merits. Some he has appointed to be ruled and governed — for whom this is more useful — so that by the word and work of those who rule they may be trained in what is profitable; others he has given as shepherds and teachers for the perfecting of the church, namely those who, endowed beyond the rest with strength of soul, stand nearer to God and perform in the church that office which either the soul performs in the body or the mind and reason in the soul, so that both, joined together alike and mingled with each other, with harmony made by the Spirit, as in the diversity of members, between what is lacking in one and what abounds in another, the body may be perfect and whole and fitted for all things, and worthy to have Christ as its head.

4. Although, then, I know that it is not safe even for any other living creatures to be without rulers and guidance, yet it is much less so for human beings, because a greater and more serious danger hangs over them when they go astray; since, if the first thing cannot be preserved in them, that they should not do wrong, this at least holds the second place of salvation in them, that they be corrected and called back from wrongdoing. If, then, this has appeared true and seemed good and just, it is certain that it is bad and useless on the contrary either for all to wish to become rulers, so that no one remains who ought to be ruled, or again for no one to wish to undertake the office of ruling, by which the whole body of the church would surely at once be able to limp and totter, with no one, that is, guiding it. And where then, or how, or by whom will God be worshipped by us? In what way will the most holy mysteries be celebrated after the likeness of the heavenly image, through which, while still placed on earth, we are joined to the heavenly orders? Without doubt what has been said will come to pass, that there will be no king nor prince nor priesthood nor sacrifice. And all those things will befall us too for which that former people was condemned on account of their immense crimes.

5. But not even this is new or strange to those among whom the pursuits of divine philosophy flourish, that someone from the rank of disciples should be taken up into the office of masters, just as [it is not strange] for a capable sailor, if the situation demands, to be transferred to the watch at the prow, or from that place, if he has properly acquired the knowledge of the winds, to be called to the very helm of the ship; or for the care of a squadron and cohort to be entrusted to a very brave soldier, or for one who commands a squadron well to be transferred to the command of the whole army. Let no one, then, of those who become very severe censors of others' affairs and weigh others' deeds by their own vices, suppose that I was ashamed of the rank of this ministry because I desired greater things. I am not so ignorant either of the greatness of divine things or of the lowliness of human things as not to judge it a great thing for the whole of mortal nature to draw near, in whatever way and in whatever rank, to God, who alone dwells in light inaccessible to every creature.

6. What, then, is the reason for my disobedience? For at that time I strove to have nothing of my own nor anything like my usual character, but to speak against [it] rather boldly and to resist rather shamelessly. Hear, then, the causes of this, which you have long been wanting. The chief cause of my disturbance was this, that it came upon me suddenly. And just as, when some sudden sound has crashed out, minds are thrown into confusion, struck by unforeseen terror, so I too, terrified, cast off all the modesty which has always been my inseparable companion throughout my whole life. Then, next, the remembrance of my silence and quiet disturbed me more violently, when I saw that hindered for me which from the beginning of my life I had singularly loved and, in great and very great dangers, had vowed to God. I was stirred by longing for it all the more because I now seemed to myself to have reached at least its door, and I was kindled the more keenly from the time its goods became better known to me. And therefore I did not bear being dragged by force into the midst of the crowds of the peoples and being thrown, as it were from some temple of quiet, into the tumultuous crashes of this life.

7. For nothing truly seemed to me more excellent for the blessed life than that someone, with the fleshly senses as it were shut, and having come to be outside the flesh and the world, should be turned in upon himself, that is, should look upon his own senses and mind and, made a stranger to the cares of mortals, should speak to himself alone and to God, so that, made higher than all visible things, he may fill his mind with divine perceptions and heavenly forms without any earthly admixture, made truly a spotless mirror of the image of God and always receiving light from his light, bearing in himself certain auspices or beginnings of the age to come and, while still placed on earth, enjoying in some way the fellowship of the angels, and, having despised and left behind earthly frailty, should be carried over to the things above and heavenly by the uplifting of the Holy Spirit. If any of you has perhaps at some time felt the ardour of a love of this kind, he knows what I am saying and recognises what I speak of and understands why I was disturbed, and will readily grant pardon. But to the rest I shall not be excessive in giving satisfaction, to whom perhaps speech of this kind, while its work is unknown, may even be an object of derision, and especially to those in whom the sickness of envy hinders the sense of judging rightly; and they inflict a vicious name on the best work, calling philosophy vainglory and defaming the splendid pursuits of wisdom with the names of boastfulness, to which the agreement of the base and unskilled multitude also gladly attaches itself. For the crowd of the unskilled is readier to disparage good pursuits than to imitate them, so that they are at fault in every way, either while they do not avoid manifest and public evils or while they do not believe in hidden and secret goods.

8. To these was added also this — for I shall set out everything before you and shall now hide nothing secret — and whether it was due to my rusticity or my frankness, you judge. I was ashamed on account of certain men whom I saw to have gained nothing at all towards the amendment of their life, nothing of correction in their morals, but rather to have become even worse, rushing in rivalry with unclean feet, as the saying goes, into the holy places and, before they were held worthy of the first approach and the doors, straightway making for the tribunal and hastening to the priesthood and, having pushed the rest aside, themselves lying upon the sacred altars, so that that order no longer seems to be for offering a pattern and example to the people, but a kind of opportunity for living in abundance and security, nor is it considered an office answerable to the future judgement of God, but is thought a secure administration never to be examined. And these rulers are almost more in number than those whom they rule, so that that saying of the apostle is nowhere, where he says: Not all are prophets, not all are teachers. For here all are teachers, all are prophets, so that according to the ancient proverb it may rightly be said that Saul too is among the prophets. And indeed no history of the ancients has handed down to us that there was ever so great a number of ministers in the church or one gathered so cheaply. Hence reproach also arises against our religion and doctrine, because priesthoods or ministries are conferred by ambition and for favour rather than by judgement of merits. Even if to prevent the vice or stain of this thing is beyond us, yet at least to be ashamed of it and to turn away from it is some part of piety.

9. But what deterred me more than everything and beyond all that we have said above is this — for I must come to the very summit of the discourse and set out what is true; for it is not right to deceive in such matters —: I judged, as I judge now too, that it is not the same to rule flocks or herds and to be over men and to govern souls. For there the effort is to make the flock, whether of the herd or of the sheep, strong in limb and fat in flesh; looking to this, the herdsman or shepherd chooses fields leafy with grass and green with streams, which he has found more fertile for pasture, and renews these very fields by alternate grazing and moves the flock from some glades to others. He also seeks out wooded resting-places for repose. He drives the flock at times with a rod, but chiefly soothes it with the sweetness of the reed or pipe. Nor does any further work weigh on the herdsman or the shepherd, except that some small care is required against the ambushes and wickedness of wolves and, if a beast is perhaps sick somewhere, to look after it with the eye or tend it by handling, to provide shade in the heat, to furnish soft and grassy beds for those lying down, and to let the place where they lie be blown through by breathing breezes, a place which the cold water of a stream running past may graze, and also to sing to the flocks, as it were, something either of antiquity or of love. Besides this, he may either slaughter whichever is fatter or turn it into money, but no care for virtue of soul and diligence weighs on shepherds of this kind, by which they would be obliged to serve the pleasure of the flock rather than their own.

10. But since it is very difficult for a man to know how to be ruled, that is, to obey the one ruling him, it is much more difficult to know how to rule others, and to rule according to this discipline of ours, which comes down from the divine law and leads to God. The greater its hope and glory, the heavier also its danger, at least for those who have understanding. Such a ruler, first of all, as it seems to me, ought to be tested like silver or gold and examined from every side and observed at every time and in his acts, lest he perhaps have within himself some foreign admixture or baser material and give back the harsh sound of bronze or an admixture of lead, and something counterfeit lie hidden within, which fire would test and dissolve. This evil will surely become the more pernicious the more numerous the people of whom he has become ruler, just as it is certainly graver for a plague to be spread among many than for one person to be consumed by pestilence.

11. Nor is the stench of a corpse so pernicious if it pollutes one place, as if, its cruel reek diffused far and wide, it breeds the disease of corrupted air for many. So, if there is any disease of vices in a ruler, it is easily passed on and poured over into those who stand ready to obey him; and what is evil passes from him much more easily than whatever of virtue and diligence there may be in him. In this matter I too, often conferring with myself about such things, am accustomed to wonder greatly that wickedness advances so easily and without any labour or any aids, and nothing is so easy as to become evil, even if no one teaches, no one compels, while it is rare and very difficult to become good, and as if the ascent of some steep and precipitous rock had to be climbed, though many call one on, though many invite, even if all favour and urge. And this is what it seems to me blessed Haggai too understood when he introduced that admirable picture of questioning, when it is said to him: Ask the priests the law and say to them: If holy flesh or a holy vessel touches anyone's garment, does it sanctify it from the fact that it touched it? And when the priests had said that it does not sanctify, he says to them again: If uncleanness touches the garment of a clean man, does it pollute it? And they said that it pollutes.

12. This, then, is what our discourse here too has now reviewed: that the taking up of good is very difficult for mortal nature, as if fire were applied to some damp material. But very many of us are ready and apt to receive evil, as if someone were to throw a spark of fire onto dry stubble, which moreover is fanned by blowing winds. So we are more quickly consumed by a small spark of wickedness than we can be kindled or even warmed by the fires of virtue. For a little wormwood thrown into much honey imparts a swift bitterness, but even if double the honey is thrown into wormwood, sweetness will not be able to prevail over it. So a small clod withdrawn from a river's bank draws off the weight of the whole river headlong, but to withstand and turn aside the river's fall you could scarcely do with great masses and immense engines.

13. For this reason, first of all, we must fear lest we be found to be certain very bad painters of beautiful and comely virtue, or at least lest we offer very bad models of its image to other painters, that is, to the people, who ought to paint it in themselves; or at least lest there happen to us the matter of the common proverb, that we who preside over the healing of others are found ourselves teeming with sores.

14. Then next, even if someone guards himself from the contamination of all sin, I do not think even this is enough for one who presides over peoples to be educated and trained in virtue. For it is not enough that he to whom the chief charge of teaching is entrusted should not be evil — which is certainly blameworthy and shameful even in those who are taught — but he ought also to be endowed with all good acts, according to that command which says: Turn aside from evil and do good. Nor is it enough to cast unworthy thoughts out of the soul and to wipe out the forms of evil things, but [one must] also implant and inscribe more excellent and more divine ones, so that virtue of mind may seem to have been acquired by us much more than human rank. Nor should we ever think that any end of good deeds or limit of progress has been set for us, nor should what we have done rightly be counted as gain so much as what we have not yet been able to fulfil should be reckoned as loss. And this life should be thought of by us as a kind of ascent, from which it matters nothing to have completed what you have climbed unless you get past what remains. Nor let us measure ourselves by comparison with others and think it a great thing if perhaps we are found more excellent than some, but rather let us consider it a loss if we do not act in a manner worthy of our place and rank; and if anything is done by us, let it be weighed not by comparison with the negligent but by the authority of the precept, whether those others live more negligently or even somewhat more zealously, because we have received the forms of the virtues not from the deeds of our neighbours but from the authority of the word of God, from whom are all things, and in whom are all things, and to whom all things are referred.

15. Nor should it be thought that the same things suit everyone, just as neither is there one age for all, nor are the features of faces the same for everyone, nor is there one quality of the whole earth, nor one brightness of the stars. It should be thought fitting, then, for the unlearned and any simpler person not to act wrongly and to beware of doing anything that leads to punishment or is struck by the most severe censure of the law. But for him who presides over others it is fitting, having left behind every work of sin, to advance in the best things, so that by the example of his progress he can invite and entice the rest to virtue, chiefly through the pattern of humility handed down to us by the Lord. For one ought not to constrain by force or necessity, but persuade by reason and the examples of one's life, because whatever is extorted from the unwilling, along with seeming tyrannical, cannot even last. For whatever is drawn by violence usually, like the top of a young tree if someone bends it by force, returns again, once released, to what it was. But what is done by purpose and will is as lawful as it is sure, being bound, that is, by the very strong bonds of one's own will. Hence also the apostle, writing to the Hebrews, commands to rule the flock willingly and not of necessity.

16. But there is someone who is neither evil nor has reached the summit of virtue, and I do not see with what confidence one comes to teach who has not himself approached with this faith, namely to learn. For in very truth it seems to me to be the art of arts and the discipline of disciplines to rule or to instruct man, who is certainly, among all living things, the most varied in character and diverse in will. Indeed, one will also, no less readily, consider the care of souls from the medicine of bodies, and the harder he finds bodily medicine to grasp, the harder he will find that of souls, since both the quality of the substance is far more excellent and the end of the matter far more precious. For that [medicine] provides healing to bodies and applies care and diligence to temporal matter, which without doubt will at some time be dissolved by the frailty of its nature, even if now it is repaired with the help of art. For it is certain that every body is dissolved either by sickness or by time, and is not permitted by the condition of its frailty to endure beyond the limits of its nature.

17. But the soul, which is divine and comes from God, shares in a heavenly nobility, to which it also hastens to return, although it is bound and tied to a worse partner, perhaps also for other reasons, which only God, who bound and tied it, knows, and anyone who has been enlightened and instructed by him about mysteries of this kind; but, as far as I can understand, for two reasons, I think: one, that through the struggles of the contests which it has against earthly things it may seek the inheritance of heavenly glory, and, as gold by fire, be proved by the testing of the hardships of the present life, so that it may hope for the rewards of virtue not only from God's gift but, so that virtue may truly be its highest good, may win it by its own work and labour, so that the good may seem to be naturally implanted in us by the Creator, but cultivated by us by our will and purpose and spread by the exercise of the free choice that moves in either direction; the other, that it might also draw with itself this worse substance of the body and set it on high in the heavenly seats, gradually dissolving its grossness, by which it is held back, so that what God is to the soul, the soul too may become to the body, governing matter as its servant and offering it to God with itself as a faithful fellow servant.

18. Doctors will inquire into differences of places and times and age and other such things, when and what medicines or foods are needed, or how one should abstain from harmful things, so that the discipline of the art is not overcome by the desires of the sick; at times they also use cutting with the knife and more virulent medicines. Although all these things are carried out with great labour, nothing is done in them such as it is to correct morals, purge vices, amend lives and turn one's purpose to better things, and to regulate with diligent watchfulness everything done within us or even outside us, so that, separating from our nature everything in us that is beastly and wild, we may implant in place of all those things whatever is gentle and mild, whatever is worthy of man and dear to God, and may keep a fair judgement between soul and body, never subjecting the better nature to the worse, which is surely most unjust, but always making use of the command of the mind and the service of the body. This is the first law of God, and most excellently established, to be observed throughout his whole creation, whether visible or even what exceeds the sense of sight.

19. I also consider this: that all these things which we mentioned above as observed by doctors each remain according to the order of their nature, and it can in no way happen that the doctor attempts anything either against art or against nature, since the very quality of bodily matter yields to and obeys the disciplines of medicine, unless perhaps some impatience or restlessness of the sick person should occur, which itself too is certainly not hard either to watch for or to prevent. With us, however, everything is done in the spirit, and our highest effort is to overcome those who wrongly love themselves in a carnal way and in no way wish to yield to us, fighting against themselves, so that we have a kind of war against those for whom we are campaigning, while each one puts as much effort into covering and hiding the diseases and vices of his sins as he ought to have in revealing his sickness to the doctor.

20. In this they seem to themselves brave and steadfast against their own salvation and prudent against their own life, while they hide sin within themselves and within the secret places of their mind like some theft, as though what is hidden from men could be hidden from that eye which sees all things; or while they make excuses in their sins, when for their own vices and passions they devise certain reasons and become advocates of their own evils; or at least when, in the manner of the deaf asp, which does not hear the voice of the charmers nor yield to the remedies of the wise, by which alone the sickness of the soul is cured, they do not receive the word of one admonishing them; or at least, which is the ultimate evil, when they now openly and shamelessly defend their sins and, as if out of their minds, rush headlong publicly and without shame into every disgraceful act, and then they even take revenge, as on enemies and adversaries, on those who desire somewhat to hinder or at least delay them for their salvation, hating those who rebuke in the gates and cursing the holy word, the most unhappy of all, punishing themselves the more, the more fiercely they have raged against their adversaries, like those who, seized by madness and fury, tear their own flesh, which, out of their minds, they think belongs to another.

21. These are the reasons why I think this medicine of our discipline far more difficult than that which heals bodies alone. And the more difficult it is, the more precious and useful it certainly is. For that [medicine] deals with only a few things of the deeper sort, but carries most of its art and work before the eyes and in the hands; in this one of ours, however, all care and all effort is directed toward the inner man of the heart, and against the enemy who assails us from within and struggles against us in our senses. Our whole contest is against him who, misusing us ourselves as swords against us, hands us over to death. Against all these things, then, we must strive with much faith, indeed with all faith, but with greater grace of God, and also to some degree, as I think, with our own effort and labour, which is shown in word and deed, so that we may, as is the more precious thing in us, either cure souls of the sicknesses of vices or cleanse them of the stains of sins.

22. Now the end of each medicine (for this remains to be shown) is, for the one, that the health of the body be either preserved, if it is present, or recalled, if it has departed. It is not quite certain whether this has always benefited those who have had it, since we often see that the strength of bodily vigour has harmed some, while certain people, trusting in it, give themselves to banditry or robbery. Yet these things are indifferent, like poverty and wealth, or lowliness and fame, and other things like these, which are called indifferent because, according to the purpose of those who use them, they can be drawn either to good or to evil. But the end of the other, that is, of this medicine of ours, is to rouse the soul to virtue, to snatch it out of this world and offer it to God, and either to preserve the image of God which is in it, if it is upright, or to guide it, if it is in danger, or, if it has fallen or been crushed, to restore it, Christ being implanted in hearts through the Holy Spirit, and finally to make man a son of God and to set him with the heavenly beings in heavenly blessedness.

23. For this the law was given to us as a tutor, for this the prophets were sent, between the law and Christ, for this the spiritual law is fulfilled and Christ, the end of all things, came. This is what the emptied divinity accomplishes, this is what the assumption of flesh advances, and this is what we gain from both. This is that new mingling of God and man, that through the one we may possess both. For this reason God was mingled with a body through the mediation of a soul, that he might join what was separated and call back into concord and peace what was in discord, recalling into one in himself and through himself all things that had first been betrayed by the one father of our race: he took up a soul because of the disobedience of the soul, flesh because of its evil obedience, for which it too was condemned along with it, so that, as the condemnation had been in flesh and soul, so salvation might come about in flesh and soul. Christ, then, for Adam; he who was without sin [took the place] of him who was made subject to sin.

24. And the new is brought in for the old, so that through the voluntary suffering of this one, he who had suffered unwillingly might be healed, so that, namely, what was above us might be rendered on behalf of each of us. So the new mystery of mercy is fulfilled toward him who fell through disobedience. For this reason [there is] a new birth, and a virgin mother, and Bethlehem for Eden, and a manger for paradise, small and visible things for hidden and great ones. For this reason too shepherds see the heavenly glory, because of the Lamb and Shepherd; for this reason the magi, led by a star, worship and offer gifts, so that no one should any longer worship either idols or stars; for this reason Jesus is baptised and testimony is borne to him from heaven, and he fasts and is tempted and conquers him who had conquered; for this reason demons are put to flight, sicknesses are cured, and the preaching of great things is entrusted to the least.

25. For this reason the nations rage and the peoples meditate vain things; for this reason wood [is set] against wood, and hands are patiently stretched out against hands intemperately stretched out: in place of loose and slack ones, hands fixed with nails are offered; in place of those which cast out Adam, hands are offered which embrace the whole world and call it back. Exaltation is taken up for lowliness, the taste of gall for the sweet and deadly taste, and death is exchanged for death, darkness for darkness, burial for burial, resurrection for resurrection. All these things are a certain care of God toward us and a medicine for our weakness, restoring and reshaping the old Adam to the state from which he fell, and returning him to the tree of life, from which the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, taken untimely and out of season, had driven us.

26. Of this medicine and cure, then, we are ministers and helpers, all of us who are seen to preside over peoples. And I do not know whether we have advanced even so far as to be able to cure our own weaknesses, let alone to treat the sicknesses of others and to cleanse the stains of souls by careful instruction.

27. Then again, doctors of bodies endure labour, sleepless nights and anxieties, and, as one of the wisest of them says, bear others' misfortunes with griefs of their own, themselves seeking out and finding some things for healing by their own labour, borrowing others from others, and there is absolutely nothing that escapes them. They neglect not even the smallest thing, but reckon as great and supreme everything that contributes anything to the health of the body, thinking it the highest good if they seem through their diligence to contribute something to this life which we lead on earth, and sometimes to the life of the worst of men, for whom it would long since have been a common good to depart from this world. And even if by these means they provide for the life of good men, how much is that which is conferred by it, when the very length of years and old age soon brings it to an end! For what does any good man gain from this life, when it is certain that no wise man ought to love what he will in any case soon leave behind?

28. But we, for whom the danger concerns the salvation of souls, for whom the contest is for immortality and the struggle is over an eternity either of glory or of punishment (of which virtue will prepare the one, sloth the other), how much labour and effort must we undertake, how much diligence or virtue must we apply, so that, cured of vices, amended in morals, corrected in purpose, we may both transfer our life from present things to future ones and subject and submit the earth to the spirit! Just as, then, not one kind of medicine is applied to all, so neither does the same speech suit everyone; the same approach does not fit a woman and a man, or an old man and a young one, nor the poor and the rich, the joyful and the sad, the sickly and the vigorous, rulers and subjects, the wise and the unskilled, the timid and the bold, the irascible and the gentle, those advancing and those declining.

29. And to search still deeper, the same things will not suit those who are in marriage and those who are free from the marriage yoke. But among these too there is again a difference, between those who lead their life in deserts and those who have a common way of life, mixed with others. And again, the same things will not fit those who are reasoning in faith and perceptive in the scriptures and those who advance by simplicity alone, nor those who come down from city life and those who come from a rural and rustic one; not the same for the simple and the shrewd, nor for those engaged in business and those living far from it and at rest, nor for those who have turned after the blows of sins and those who chose good things before experiencing evil. Among each of these a great difference must be observed, since their very impulses and desires also bear very many differences among themselves. Finally, consider it again from the bodily account of the elements: although we all subsist from the same elements, yet each body has a certain temperament of its own.

30. And for this reason the same medicines do not benefit all, but one needs one medicine or food or drink, another another, and different things suit different individuals. So also a varied and diversely composed speech will cure souls. And those very people who have experienced it will be my witnesses to these things: that some are amended by speech alone, others are converted by examples; some must be roused with goads, others restrained with reins, because some are slower and sluggish toward good work (who are fittingly stirred by the lashes of words), while others, too much stirred by fervent spirit, exceed the measure of fairness, as when a spirited and fiery colt, still impatient of the yoke through its newness, spills in a wanton course beyond the set bounds of the turning-posts; these speech will better temper, reining them in and calling them back to the fixed lines of the commandments.

31. For many it has been beneficial to be praised, for others to be censured; yet both [only] if they are offered at the right time; otherwise, offered unseasonably, they have rather done harm. Some a consoling speech has corrected, others a rebuke; and for some it is fitting to be reproved before everyone, for others to be admonished more privately. For some despise more private warnings but blush at public disgrace; others, however, when confronted publicly, become more shameless, while they revere the secret mystery of a private rebuke and repay their obedience, as a kind of gift, for an honourable and attentive service.

32. For some it is fitting that everything be watched more carefully and examined down to the least detail, especially those who, while they think they are hiding their evils by some skill, are lifted up against others and puffed up; for others, however, it is right to pass over some things, so that seeing we may seem not to have seen, and hearing not to have heard, according to the saying of the proverb, so that they may not come through rebuke to ultimate contempt, those who perhaps are ashamed to extend and multiply their faults as long as they think them unknown, but become bold and headlong once their shame, the last and only remedy for amendment, has been broken off. Sometimes, too, we must be angry with some without being angry, and despise some yet not despising, and despair not despairing, since the character of each one requires it so; others, again, we must cure with gentleness, others with humility, namely by joining ourselves to them and promising one and the same rule of hope. And to conquer some, but to be conquered by others, has sometimes been better; and it is sometimes fitting to praise and embrace the prosperity and power of some, but the poverty and lowliness of others.

33. For it is not as with the order and nature of virtue and sloth, that the one is always praised and the other always blamed; our discipline's order does not likewise demand that a sick soul always receive what is sound and useful and fitting—for example, either to be rebuked more sharply or admonished more gently, or always to choose one of all the things we mentioned above—but this can be received by some, and the contrary by others, as the time or the matter or the very sickness of souls permits. But to distinguish everything in speech and set it out in detail, so as to describe in order every care of healing, I think impossible even for those who have deserved to know the secrets of wisdom itself.

34. But as far as has been revealed to us through the word of God and brief experience has been able to discover, I think this must be observed as a general aim: just as for those whose skill is to walk along ropes stretched on high, to lean this way or that is perilous, and to stray a little, however very slight that may seem, is death, but all their safety lies in this, that they keep the taut and straight line of their step, so also in these actions of ours, to whatever side anyone leans for whatever cause, whether he does it from malice or from inexperience, it is a matter of the utmost danger. And if he is also in charge of others, he will become the cause of eternal ruin not for himself alone but for the others too. Therefore one must walk on the royal road and attend neither to the things on the right nor to those on the left, as the proverbial saying warned beforehand. Let it suffice, then, to have mentioned these things about our vices and passions and what work they demand for their cure from the good shepherd, namely from him who, according to the saying of scripture, knowingly knows the souls of his flocks and rules the flock according to the Lord's word and the pastoral discipline which we have received from Christ, the true shepherd of all.

35. But how shall I be able to explain the very care of the word of God and the principle of teaching—to speak last of what is first and great—since today, as I see, all are teachers and all philosophise? At which I wonder greatly, whether all these whom I see in the church coming forward to deliver a sermon to the people know well and rightly how to give their fellow servants their measure of wheat in due season, and to order their words with judgement, and to explain coherently and rationally the truth of our doctrines: whatever must be philosophised about worlds or the world, about matter, about the soul, about the mind, about intellectual natures, whether good or contrary, and—what is greatest, and what binds, holds together and orders all things—about providence and about the particular things which seem to happen either against reason (human reason, that is) or according to reason.

36–37. And also how one should think about our first state and final restoration, about prefigurations and the truth, about both testaments, about the first and second coming of Christ, about his incarnation and passion and resurrection and ascension into heaven, about the end of all things, about judgement, about the requital of sorrows or of good things, and above all, and what is first, about the blessed Trinity that holds the beginning of all things. In this lies the height of danger for those who preside over enlightening others: lest anyone, his speech contracted into one subsistence and person, as if avoiding a multitude of gods, should think there are only appellations of names and, supposing the same one to be named Father and Son and Holy Spirit, should fall away into the impiety of Sabellius through such confusion and mixture, so that, while he thinks all are named one, he makes each one to be nothing, since what is ceases to be when what is said to be each one's own is poured over into the other—or indeed, which is absurd, a God composed of different parts is introduced to us, according to those popular fables in which one animal is sketched and painted out of different forms—; nor again [lest they] cut up the nature of God according to the madness of Arius and, shutting up the abundance of the Godhead within Jewish poverty, ascribe the fullness of deity to the unbegotten Father alone, as if fearing that a corruption of deity might seem to occur for us if God the Father is [father] of a true God, a Son equal to himself by nature; nor [lest they] put forward three beginnings of deity, contrary to one another and different, so that through many principles they seem to return again to the errors of the pagans, from which they had departed.

38. Nor is it right for the Godhead to be divided into three substances alien from one another and different, according to Arius. For no one ought to think he so defers to God the Father as to take from him that very thing which he is, Father—for whose father will he be, if the nature of the Son is separated from him and joined to the rest of creatures? For to be Son is neither to be estranged from the Father nor to be mingled and poured back into the Father—nor again think he acts for Christ in such a way that not even to him is it preserved to be what he is, Son; for whose son will he be, if his origin is not referred to the Father, so that the one is he who begot and the other he who is begotten from him? For the Father is the origin not of something slight and unworthy, but he is the origin of Godhead and goodness, which is understood and perceived in the Son and the Holy Spirit: in the one as Son and Word, in the other as Spirit proceeding from him. And so it is necessary both that we confess one God according to the truth of substance and that we perceive Father and Son and Holy Spirit each to subsist in his own substance.

39. I have perhaps drawn these things out more than the time allowed, wishing to show the life, speech and understanding of him who presides over peoples, so that, perfected in both, he may become a dwelling of the Holy Spirit, through whom alone God is understood and interpreted and heard. For it belongs to the pure to touch the pure, and to the holy to know holy things. And this must be known first of all: that it is a very difficult task, in a mixed and varied multitude, where age and training differ, for one discussing such matters, and as it were striking a lyre of many strings, to find and bring forth a word of preaching fit for all, and so to apply the plectrum to each that the sound nowhere offends the hearing. For the danger of those who speak in the church hangs on three things: on understanding, on word, on hearing, so that it very easily happens that one slips in at least one of them, if not in all. For either the understanding is less enlightened, or sufficient speech was lacking to explain, or a duller hearing did not receive what was well delivered; and from any one of these mishaps comes danger to the truth in all. And indeed in other studies and disciplines speech is easily delivered or received, but in these schools of ours the very expectation of the hearers creates danger for the one who is to speak.

For as people about to hear about God and to receive a word concerning the highest hope and salvation of all, the warmer they are towards the faith, the more attentive and scrupulous they become towards hearing, so that, if anywhere the speech of the speaker has sounded at all amiss, they do not think it a slip of the tongue but condemn it as a betrayal of faith and piety. And they judge everything not by the reasoning of the teacher but by their own notions, keeping not the doctrines they hear in the church but those they bring with them from home, not those they have learned by reason but those they have held from a custom not to be approved. And this I call the fault of men not yet very bad, who, although they do not hold the rule of truth, nevertheless seem to suffer this out of religious feeling, and to have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; and therefore perhaps they will seem not to deserve too severe condemnation, as those who will not be beaten with many stripes, being ignorant of the Lord's will and for that reason not doing it; or [they are men] who perhaps may even at some time be corrected and amended, since a religious mind, as quickly as it is offended, is as readily and easily healed. If perhaps a word fittingly and suitably applied to them strikes the heart, at once, like a fire-bearing stone struck by one like it, from the spark of light naturally within it, it immediately kindles torches of truth.

But what shall we say of those who, while they seek the glory of boasting and delight in presiding over the people, speak iniquity on high, who like some Jannes and Jambres resist not so much Moses as the truth, and move the weapons of words against sound doctrine? There is also a third kind, of those who speak against out of ignorance, an ignorance which insolence naturally accompanies; and they meet every word with hostility and insolence, unless perhaps it is one they have put forward themselves. By these, according to the Lord's saying, the pearls of truth are trampled underfoot in the manner of swine.

There are also others who bring no opinion from their own understanding, nor hold any form of faith in God, either good or bad, but hand themselves over to all teachers and receive every discourse, as if they were going to choose from all what is better and more correct, not knowing that they have chosen poor judges of the truth, namely themselves, and that they think they can judge things which they admit they do not know. Then, often turned and changed by plausible arguments, now towards this, now towards that, and now acquiescing in every word, a little later resisting again, they change both teachers and pursuits together, and like dust stirred by the wind they are easily carried off. But at last they produce the fruit of their folly; for as if wearied by hearing different men and overcome by tedium, they reject everything at once, and, having been made as it were empty and void of all that they believed, they immediately begin even to despise and mock us, as having nothing reasonable in our faith; and they suffer what usually happens to those who have sore eyes and blame the light of the sun, or [sore] ears, and complain that men's voices are not loud enough.

For this reason, then, it is far more useful for a soul to receive the elements of truth simply and purely, and to inscribe them as on wax not yet written upon, than to write over what was badly written before, that is, to press the word of faith and truth upon bad teaching and perverse doctrines and to confuse the last with the first. For it is better to walk a road worn and smoothed by the constant passage of travellers than one unused and rough and trodden by no previous footsteps; and it is better to sow a field tamed by the exercise of frequent ploughing than one which knows no furrow and is ignorant of the ploughshare; and I would better cultivate that soul which has not yet been violated by the plough of any malicious cultivator, nor taken over beforehand by the worst seed. Otherwise our labour will be doubled, since it is necessary first to thrust out of the heart the forms of wickedness conceived earlier, and then to reshape the image of goodness with the varied waxes of the virtues, so that as many and various as the kinds of depravity were in the soul, so many may be [the kinds] of restoration. The knowledge and discipline of all these things ought to flourish in him to whom the care of instructing souls is entrusted. Of these we now pass over very many for the sake of brevity.

For just as, for example, if it could happen that out of many animals and little beasts, differing in kind and species, large and small, fiercer and milder, rougher and gentler, some one animal or one beast were made up, and if this were entrusted to someone to tame, how much work and labour would face him, how much diligence would be required of him, to meet each of the beasts or animals as the habit of each demands or as its nature requires! Since indeed neither is the same voice suited to all, nor are they driven by the same whistles, so to speak. Nor is the food one and the same for all, nor is there one way of stroking and caressing the beasts, so that sometimes by the very same things by which some are calmed others are roused to fury. In what ways, then, will that trainer adapt himself to each of the parts of this beast? How will he accommodate himself to the nature and temperament of each? Will it not be necessary for him, though he is in himself simple and constant, to become as varied and as changeable into different forms as the very diversity of the beasts demands, so that each animal may be treated according to what suits its nature and temperament, in order that the body of the whole beast, composed of such great diversity, may rightly remain in peace and tranquillity, the little beasts being kept in check among themselves? So he who has undertaken to instruct and rule this common body of the church, made up as it were into one animal out of many and diverse customs, tongues and trainings, and unlike itself, though he himself ought always to be unmoved and the same in himself, must nevertheless conform himself to the customs and trainings of each, and fit his speech suitably to each.

Since indeed some need milk, namely those to whom the first rudiments of religion are still being delivered, and, being little ones in faith, cannot yet bear the strength of manly food, so to speak; and if anyone pressed this on them beyond their strength, perhaps, overwhelmed and weighed down, since the mind is not equal to receiving what is pressed on it—just as not even in little children can the bodily substance digest foods too great for its strength—they will suffer the loss and damage even of what they had before. But there are others who need wisdom, which is spoken and preached among the perfect, and they can use loftier and stronger foods, because they have their senses trained to discern good and evil, truth and falsehood. For these it is not fitting to be given milk to drink or to be fed on vegetables, that is, on weak and frail food; otherwise they will by no means be strengthened in the strength of Christ, nor grow with that praiseworthy increase by which every perfect man ought to grow in him into a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ.

And who is sufficient for these things? For we ought not to be like many, adulterating the word of God and mixing water with wine, that is, mixing with the word that gladdens the heart of man a cheap discourse that creeps along the ground, which either raises a joke or tells of some temporal thing, so that we seem to be trading for some fleshly gain from it, when we speak to each as they themselves delight to hear, and are like certain ventriloquists, that is, speaking from the belly and for the belly, and providing for the belly in all our words, which is truly to speak of the earth, so that we may seem to please the powerful and the rich, whom we rather harm, indeed whom we destroy, and whose innocent blood we shed, that is, we give over to destruction the life of simple souls, which will surely be required at our hands.

For all these reasons, then, I considered it much better to yield the reins of governing to others more skilled than to drive the chariot headlong through lack of skill, and rather to bend the ear to hearing in obedience than to move an unskilled tongue. Discussing these things with myself, and using myself as a counsellor not a bad one, as I think, or, if not that, at least a diligent one, I preferred, being ignorant, to learn rather than to teach the words and deeds that pertain to piety. For it is desirable and very dear to me to learn until extreme old age, since indeed no age can suffice for learning thoroughly; but for one who is not sufficiently instructed to aspire to teach others seems to me a matter of the old proverb, 'to learn the potter's craft on a wine-jar', that is, to learn the teaching of piety at the peril of souls. And such people seem to me either quite foolish or rash: foolish, if they are so dull as not to perceive that they are unskilled; rash, if they do understand it, yet dare to undertake the task.

Elders of the Hebrews hand down that among them in ancient times there was a certain praiseworthy custom of this kind: not every scripture was entrusted to every age to be read or learned, because it was not expedient for all to learn everything quickly, since not all can grasp everything either, and therefore they would be harmed rather than helped if, while not yet capable, they came to know the things that are deeper. All the rest, whose historical narrative is also not objectionable, they learn straight away from boyhood; but those scriptures which under the cheap garment of the letter cover precious mysteries within, no one is allowed to learn or even to know before the twenty-fifth year, so that this may be set out as a kind of reward for the exercise of virtue to those in whom, by that age, an approved life, good conduct and capacity of understanding become apparent; who can by then rise well and confidently from the lower things of the letter to the higher and lofty things of the spirit.

What then? Among us will there be no difference, no distinction, between teaching and being taught? Will no division be made between tribe and tribe? Will those not receive their inheritance by lot beyond the Jordan and these within the Jordan? Will no boundary mark be given to our peoples? Will no rule of living be fixed, but will everything be held in such confusion, and will each one do what seems right in his own eyes, so that very many of us, not to say all, almost before we shed the first down of infancy, while we still lisp like children, having scarcely entered the Lord's halls, before we know even the very names of the sacred books, before we learn either the authors or come to know the style of the New or Old Scripture—for I do not say, before we wash off the filth and put away the vices of the soul—if perhaps we have somewhere learned two or three discourses from the ancient commentators, and that perhaps more by hearing than by reading, or if we have learned a few of David's psalms here and there, and then wear a darker and well-arranged garment, or if we even display philosophy as far as the belt of our girdle, colouring for ourselves an appearance and face of piety with devices of this kind, at once we want to be admired and praised, we think already of presiding over peoples, we seem to ourselves some Samuels consecrated from the very cradle, wise men too, and teachers and initiates of divine things, and we rank ourselves among the scribes and doctors of the law, and walk about like some heavenly beings, seeking to be called rabbi by men, saying: 'The letter is never to be accepted at all, but everything is to be understood spiritually'—otherwise it would seem to be ravings and dreams—and on top of this we are indignant unless we are praised vehemently and with applause? And these are the kindlier and simpler among us; but those 'spiritual' men, disdainful, judging and condemning each person and counting them altogether as nothing, if they so please, even withdraw, refusing our communion as impious.

But if we wish to approach one of them with gentler admonitions and to meet him with reasoned argument, saying: 'I beg you, best of men, answer me: do you consider playing the pipe or striking the lyre to be an art or discipline?', without doubt he will admit it is a discipline. 'What then do you think of the wise man and of wisdom itself, that is, of the discipline and knowledge of divine and human things?' They will grant this too. 'And what then? Do we consider those arts better than wisdom, or that wisdom far surpasses all of them?' I know that they will grant this too; and so far they will keep faith in the truth of their answers. What then? Shall the discipline of the lyre and the pipe have its teaching and instructions, and shall time be given for learning it, and labour and study be applied, and fees be paid to teachers, and sometimes even, if a more skilled master is heard of anywhere, shall a long journey abroad also be undertaken for this, and whatever pertains to a polished education, even if it is costly, be borne and done; but wisdom, which is both chief and discoverer of all things, and has and contains all things in itself, by whose name God too delights to be called rather than by the other titles which human speech may rightly use—shall we think it so light and of so little weight as to suppose that anyone has only to wish it and is at once wise? Is this not the mark of utter and hopeless ignorance? If, then, we put such arguments to them, or ones like these, or even stronger, we are sowing on rocks among them and telling tales to deaf ears, so that they are not wise even in this, that at least when admonished they recognise their ignorance. Hence it seems to me that the saying of Solomon is fittingly and suitably applied to them, where he says: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun: a man who seems wise in his own eyes. But this is without doubt far worse, if one who does not know himself to be unskilled is even appointed teacher of others.

This sickness needs great tears and mourning rather than words. Hence I too have often pitied such men within myself, knowing that to wish to seem wise is to be not wise at all. But a great hindrance to men on the way to virtue is the presumption of false and empty glory. To escape the stain of this disease completely is perhaps for a Peter or a Paul, who, though they had been found worthy to receive from Christ the grace of the word and of wisdom and of governing, nevertheless became all things to all, that they might gain all. For us, however, it is enough if we at least allow ourselves to be rightly governed and ruled by those to whom the grace of ruling and governing has been granted.

But since we have mentioned Paul and others like him, let us leave aside, if you will, all the others who presided over peoples either through lawgiving or through prophecy or through command in war or through some charge of this kind, such as Moses or Aaron or Joshua or Elijah or Elisha and all the judges, Samuel too and David and the rest of the multitude of the prophets, John the Baptist as well, and also the twelve disciples of the Lord and those who, either with them or after them, presided over peoples each in his own time with much labour and sweat; leaving all these aside for the present, we shall call on Paul alone in support of our argument, and in him and through him we shall consider what and how great a thing is the care and diligence of souls, or whether it requires little effort and prudence or demands little counsel and labour. Let us see, then, what Paul says of Paul, and learn from him what this business is that is under discussion.

I pass over listing his labours and vigils, the miseries endured in thirst and hunger, in cold and nakedness; I pass over those who lay in wait without and those who resisted within; I pass over persecutions, Jewish councils, prisons, chains, accusers, trials, deaths daily and at every moment; that he was let down through the wall in a basket, that he was stoned, that he was beaten with rods; I pass over his journeys round the world, dangers at sea, dangers on land, a day and a night in the deep, shipwrecks, dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from his own race, dangers among false brothers, a living sought by the labour of his hands, the gospel without charge; that he became a spectacle both to men and to angels, he who stood midway between God and men, enduring contests and struggles on behalf of men, and gathering and acquiring for God a people of his own. Besides all these things, then, who could worthily set forth his daily provision for each one and his anxiety for all the churches? Compassionate towards all, stretched by brotherly affection towards all: someone suffered a stumbling, and Paul was weak; another was made to stumble, and Paul burned.

But shall I list his zeal and labour in teaching? Or the variety of his cares? Or shall I speak of his gentleness and again his severity, or the blend of the two, so that he neither inflamed by much harshness nor slackened by excessive kindness? He gives laws to slaves and masters, rulers and subjects, husbands and wives, parents and children, married and unmarried, the continent and the self-indulgent, the wise and the unwise, circumcision and uncircumcision, the Church and the world, the spirit and the flesh. For some he rejoices and gives thanks, others he chastises and rebukes; some he calls his joy and crown, others he brands with folly; with some who run well he runs, others who run badly he reins in and calls back. Now he separates from the Church, now he receives back and confirms love; now he mourns some, now he is gladdened by others; now he gives milk to drink, now he reveals mysteries; now he lowers himself and makes himself equal to the lowly, now he raises the lowly with himself and exalts them; now he puts forward a spirit of gentleness, now he threatens the proud and arrogant with the rod of apostolic power; now he rises against those who are lifted up, now he becomes to his disciples as if a nurse cherishing her little ones; now he is the least of all the apostles, now he promises proof of himself through Christ who speaks in him; now he longs to depart and be with Christ, now he judges it necessary to remain in the flesh for the sake of those who need it; for he does not seek his own things, but seeks the things of his children, whom he begot in Christ through the gospel. This above all must be observed by those who preside over spiritual peoples, that in all things they neglect and disregard their own for the benefit of others.

So Paul boasts, but in his weaknesses and tribulations, and he is adorned with the dying of Christ as with some precious necklace; he is lifted above all that is carnal, but exults and boasts in spiritual things; and though he is not unskilled in knowledge, yet he says that he sees through a glass and in a riddle. He trusts in the Spirit, and yet he afflicts his body, destroying it as a hidden adversary, teaching and instructing us by these things nothing other than not to presume on anything of the things that are below, nor to be puffed up through knowledge, nor to raise up the flesh against the spirit. So he fights for all, prays for all, is jealous for all with the jealousy of God, is kindled and inflamed for all, for those who are outside the law, for those who are under the law, teacher of the Gentiles, advocate of the Jews. For them he even dares something beyond what is lawful, namely for his brothers according to the flesh, so that I too may dare to say something similar. He strives beyond the commandment of God; for he loves his neighbours not as himself but more than himself. In the end he prays that, even with himself cast off, they may be brought in to Christ in his place. O singular greatness of mind! O heavenly warmth of spirit! In this too he imitates Christ, who was made a curse for us, who took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses, and he chose, so to speak, to be outside godliness for the sake of godliness, while he endures to be anathema from Christ, if only they may be saved.

And why should I speak of each thing in turn? He lives not for himself but for Christ and the preaching of the word; he crucifies the world to himself and himself to the world; he counts all things small and slight in his longing for Christ. Even if he fills [the lands] round about from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum with the gospel, even if he is caught up and ascends as far as the third heaven, even if he is led into paradise and there hears words which it is not lawful for men to speak, in all these he does not boast except only in his weaknesses. But these things [belong to] Paul and to any there may be who are like him in spirit. As for us, I fear that, according to what is written, we may be certain foolish princes of Tanis, or exactors gleaning the peoples, or those who call the people blessed to lead them astray and confound the paths of their feet, or even of those of whom it is said that mockers shall rule over them and youths shall be set over them and children in understanding, we who perhaps have not even bread or clothing for this very purpose of being princes over others, or prophets teaching iniquity, and who are called blessed in vain. Certainly we fall far short of being priests who speak to the heart of Jerusalem. All these things Isaiah charges and reproaches, whose lips are purged by the Seraphim with a burning coal.

But what? Is the work so great and of such a kind, and so laborious to a feeling heart, while the danger is light or none and a fall of no account? Indeed it threatens me with much fear. On the one side blessed Hosea, saying that judgement is upon us priests and princes: for, he says, we have become a snare to the watchtower and like a net that is spread over Tabor, which is spread by those who catch human souls. He also threatens that the evil prophets must be cut down and their judges consumed by fire, and that there must be a ceasing from anointing kings and ordaining princes, since they set up kings for themselves and not through God.

On the other side blessed Micah deters [me], not bearing that Zion should be built with blood and Jerusalem with the iniquity of her princes, who judged for gifts, and whose priests answered for wages and whose prophets divined for money. For these and other like iniquities he says that Zion shall be ploughed like a field and Jerusalem shall be left like a hut in an orchard, and the mountain on which is the house of God shall be like a grove of the forest. Lamenting too that he finds scarcely anyone of those who walk uprightly, as if an ear of grain were found somewhere after the reapers or a cluster after the grape-gatherers, he nonetheless at times rebukes both princes who make demands and judges who speak words for favour, and almost exactly as blessed David cries out: Save me, Lord, for the holy man has failed.

Blessed Joel, moreover, even enjoins lamentation upon us and commands mourning to those who serve the altar, when the devastation of famine was threatening — so far are luxuries and abundance forbidden amid the want of others —; then they are ordered to sanctify a fast and proclaim a healing, and to bring in the old and the little children too, ages worthy of every compassion. They themselves too are ordered to go up to the temple and prostrate themselves in ashes and sackcloth — since indeed the land has become wretched and the libation and the sacrifice have been taken away from the house of the Lord —, so that through very great humility they might earn mercy.

And what shall I say of Habakkuk? He, using more fervent words, addressed his speech to God himself, and as if in confidence of the Lord's kindness he inveighs, so to speak, against the Lord himself on account of the iniquity of the judges, saying: How long, Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not hear? Shall I shout to you suffering violence, and you will not save? Why have you shown me toils and sorrows, that I should look upon this misery and impiety? Before my eyes judgement has been given, and the judge takes [bribes]. Therefore the law is overthrown and judgement is not carried through to its end. Then there follows, for all these things, a threat of this kind: Look, you despisers, and behold, and marvel at wonders, and be destroyed, for I am working a work. And what need is there to set out everything the threat contains? Let us pass over the somewhat grimmer parts. When, then, he had both wept over the wicked and to some extent called them back from evils, he tries to call back also the princes and evil teachers, forbidding them to give the flock muddy water to drink, that is, [teaching] that they ought to use a clear word and plain and pure doctrine, and by no means to pour out for their neighbours the drunkenness of the law, that is, the errors of bad understanding, nor to make ready their caves as dwellings for serpents and beasts, which is to cast evil thoughts into the souls of the hearers and to sink poisoned counsels in them.
