These, then, speak such things to us and about such things.

And how shall we bear Malachi, now rebuking the priests most bitterly, now also reproaching them for despising the name of the Lord? He even adds, when they ask him, In what have we despised the name of the Lord? and says: In that you have brought to the altar polluted loaves and food from plunder. And [he reproaches them] that they offered to God, the king of all, such votive victims as would not have been accepted if they had offered them to their own princes, namely lame and diseased and corrupt and polluted animals. Then too he reminds the Levites of the covenant of God — which is a covenant of life and peace —: that you should fear the Lord with fear and stand in awe before the face of his name. The law of truth, he says, was in his mouth, and iniquity was not on his lips. In peace he was directed and walked with me, and turned many from iniquity, for the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge and they shall seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord almighty. I would rather not set out the words of the curses along with these, but I fear to withhold anything from the truth. Yet I will set out as much as is sufficient and useful: No longer, he says, will I regard your sacrifices, nor will I receive them from your hands. And so greatly does the wrongdoing of priests provoke the Lord that he rejects and spurns even the sacrifices themselves.

When I recall Zechariah, I shudder at him who brings the sickle from heaven, who likewise himself testifies to many things against the priests. He even brings in Joshua himself, the high priest, in filthy garments, and when these are taken away clothes him in white and priestly ones. And whatever the angel says to him, although these things seem greater than what pertains to men and to surpass the state of human priesthood, and must therefore be covered in silence, yet in some way the devil is said to stand at the right hand even of Joshua himself and to oppose him. This certainly strikes much greater fear into me, a frail man, and warns me to caution.

And how much he accuses and blames the other shepherds, how much he chastises and rebukes them! Who is of so stony a heart and of such adamantine hardness that he does not tremble on hearing? A voice, he says, of lamenting shepherds, because their glory has become wretched: a voice of roaring lions, because they have suffered this and that. And he sets the lamentation as if present and before our eyes, and mourns those who suffer undeserved things. Then he repeats somewhat more reproachfully and continues more bitterly, saying: Feed the sheep of slaughter, which those who buy them slaughter and do not repent. And those who sell them say: Blessed be the Lord, for we have become rich. And their shepherds suffered nothing and did not grieve for them. Therefore I will no longer spare those who dwell in the land, says the Lord. And again he says: Arise, sword, against the shepherds, and strike the shepherds and rescue the sheep, and I will bring my hand upon the shepherds; and: My fury is kindled against the shepherds, and I will visit upon the lambs. He adds many things too, both against the people and against the leaders of the people, with great threats. But I fear I may seem too tiresome if I count everything over in order, and so I forbear to go through more.

64. I pass over too those two elders who are reported in Daniel, of whom the Lord had foretold: that iniquity came forth from Babylon, from the elders who seemed to govern the people. Ezekiel, indeed, I cannot pass over entirely, who sees such splendid and such magnificent things, who declares mysteries so hidden: how he commands the watchmen not to keep silent about the wickedness in the city and the sword coming upon it, because it is neither to their own advantage to keep silent, nor has it profited those who sin not to hear. For on the former is laid the penalty of their silence, and destruction does not delay for the latter.

65. And in another place too, how he brings in a kind of lament over the shepherds, saying: Woe upon woe shall come, and message upon message, and vision shall be sought from the prophet, and the law shall perish from the priest, and counsel from the elders. And again: Son of man, say to her: You are a land on which it has not rained, on which no shower has come down in the day of wrath; and in your midst your princes are like roaring lions, tearing their prey and devouring souls by their power. And a little later again: The priests, he says, despised my law and profaned my holy things; they did not distinguish between the unclean and the holy, but all things were one to them, and they veiled their eyes from my sabbaths. He threatens also to make an end of the wall and of those who daub or plaster it, who are those who sin and those who cover over and conceal their sins; which is certainly said of wicked rulers and priests, who, he says, turn aside the house of Israel according to their own heart, which is estranged in its lusts.

66. I forbear, indeed, to recall all that he says of those who feed themselves, who eat the milk and are clothed with the wool, who slaughter what is fattest and feed themselves and do not feed the sheep, who do not strengthen the weak, who do not bind up the broken, who do not call back what strays and do not seek what has perished and do not preserve what is stronger, but afflict and wear out and scatter them, so that the sheep are scattered over all the plains and over all the mountains because there are no shepherds, and the sheep become a prey to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, while there is no one to seek them or to bring them back. Hence the prophetic word also says thus: As I live, says the Lord, because these things are so and my sheep have become a prey, behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep from their hands. And he says that he will gather and restore the sheep, but that the shepherds will suffer the things that are prepared for wicked shepherds.

67. But lest, by counting over each of the sayings of the prophets one by one, I draw out my discourse too long, I will make mention of only one prophet more, namely him who was known before he was formed in the womb and was sanctified before he came forth from the belly — this is Jeremiah —, and pass over the rest. He seeks water for his head and a fountain of tears for his eyes, so that he may worthily bewail Israel, or the wickedness of those who are set over it.

68. For the Lord says to him concerning the priests: The priests did not say: Where is the Lord? And those who hold my law did not know me, and the shepherds acted impiously against me. Then he says: The shepherds [were] foolish and did not seek the Lord. And therefore the whole flock did not understand and was scattered. And again: Many shepherds have ruined my vineyard and defiled my portion, which was desirable; they have made it desolate and impassable. And again he is moved against them and says: O shepherds, who destroy and scatter the sheep of my flock! Therefore thus says the Lord against the shepherds: You have scattered my people and driven out my sheep and have not sought them. Behold, I will bring vengeance upon you according to your most wicked devices. He commands the shepherds also to howl and the rams of the sheep to mourn, because their days for slaughter are fulfilled.

69. But why do I linger, bringing forward so many things from the ancients, as if Paul's rules, which he laid down concerning bishops and presbyters, were not enough? He orders them to be watchful and sober, not given to wine, not violent, apt to teach, blameless in all things. That chapter, indeed, I do not even dare to bring forward publicly, in which the Lord, sending his disciples to preach, set out how they ought to act in each and every matter: what sort of men they themselves ought to be, what clothing and what footwear they ought to use, how unencumbered, how nearly stripped of everything, and, so to speak, heavenly they ought to go about upon the earth, so that they might teach virtue no less by the example of their life than by words, and the truth of their deeds might confirm the credibility of their sayings.

70. And this too moves me no less, when the Pharisees and scribes are rebuked, whom we certainly ought to surpass by far in virtue and righteousness. And I fear now that perhaps we surpass them in wickedness, so that even this may fittingly be said to us: 'Serpents, brood of vipers, and blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel, and whitewashed tombs, as it were unclean within and religious without, dishes clean on the outside', and whatever else was said against them or cast in their teeth.

71. Turning over these thoughts within myself day and night, I am worn down and consumed in my very marrow, so to speak, and with continual sighs I waste away in my flesh and melt away in my whole body. This anguish does not allow me to walk with chest thrust out and thrown back and with eyes raised and lofty, but it humbles my soul and contracts my mind; it lays chains and bridles on my very tongue too, and does not allow me to think how I ought to preside over others, nor how I may amend or correct others, but how I myself, if it can be done, may escape the coming wrath of the future judgement, and draw myself away a little from the son of perdition and make myself a stranger to him. For one must first be cleansed and so cleanse others, first become wise and so make others wise, be made light and so enlighten others, draw near to God and so bring others to God, be sanctified and so sanctify others, have upright hands and so stretch out a hand to the needy, be of upright counsel and so give upright counsel to others.

72. And when, they say, will these things be? — those who prefer everything to be quick rather than careful, who build as quickly as they destroy. And when, they say, will the lamp be set upon the lampstand? When will the talent be given to the money-changers? The grace of God, they say, does not need times and a long round. [So say] those who are more fervent for friendships than for religion, to whom everything deferred is slow; as if it were not better to find some prudence even in extreme old age than to press on untrained youth, since a lawful reign of short duration is far better than a tyranny of long duration, and since a small portion with justice is [far] better than many possessions with injustice. Or is not a little gold reckoned more precious than lead of great weight?

73. And every part that is pressed forward at the start will not be well directed at the end. For that which was sown on stony ground sprang up quickly, but because it had no depth of earth, it withered at once at the first heat of the sun. And the house whose foundations were not carried down to the firmness of the rock could not bear the onset of the rains and the force of the rivers. Moreover Solomon says, 'Woe to you, city, whose king is a youth'. And again: Do not be hasty in words. But if he commands us not to become hasty in words, how much less is it fitting to leap hastily into a work so great and so important! As if a teacher of truth ought to be brought forth suddenly, like something formed out of clay in a day — he who ought surely to stand by God with the angels, and with the archangels to glorify him, and to offer sacrifices to Christ on the heavenly altars, and to exercise the priesthood before him and with him, so that what has fallen away may be re-formed, so that the divine image in man may be restored, so that its inhabitants may be given back to the higher world, and — to say it all at once — so that from men they may pass into the number of gods.

74. We know whose ministers we are, and where and what sort of priesthood we exercise, where we are and whither we send those whom we prepare. We know the height of God and human weakness and the power given to weakness. Heaven is lofty, but the earth deep. And who of those who have been cast down for sin will ascend there? Who, surrounded by darkness and obscurity and wrapped in the grossness of the flesh, will with his whole mind purely behold the whole Mind? Who is there that may mingle with things that stand fast and are invisible, while he is still among the things that are seen and where nothing stands fast? For scarcely will anyone placed here, even of those who have been greatly purified, be able to see a certain image and likeness of the good, like those who gaze at the sun in water. Who then is there that can worthily behold him who has measured the water with his hand and the heaven with his palm and the whole earth with his fist, who has set the mountains on scales and the hills in a balance? What will be the place of his rest, and to whom will he be likened?

75. Who will be able to comprehend him who by Word and Wisdom fashioned man, and brought together into one and composed things at variance with one another, mingled earth with spirit, and joined together a living being visible and invisible, temporal and immortal, earthly and heavenly, touching God and not comprehending [him], drawing near and set far off? I said, says Solomon, I will become wise, and wisdom itself was made far from me, far more than it was. And he who adds knowledge will add sorrow, because the things found through knowledge do not gladden as much as those that escape and cannot be grasped bring grief, as usually happens to those from whom the cup is taken away while they are still thirsty.

76. These are the things that persuaded me that it is better to hear the voice of teachers than to become a teacher beyond my powers: if the height of heavenly beings and the purity of those above can scarcely contain the brightness of God, whose covering is the abyss, whose hiding place is darkness, though he himself is wholly light and dwells in light unapproachable, who is in all things and is outside all things, who is every good and is above every good, who enlightens the mind and escapes the mind, withdrawing as far as you have approached — in understanding, that is — so that, while he himself flees further and withdraws, he may call forth and invite his lover to the inner things, and be desired the more, while, as though already grasped, he slips away.

77. Since, then, he whom we seek and whom we desire, whom we follow and toward whom we hasten, is such and so great, what sort of man ought he to be through whom longing souls are to have access to him who is sought and desired? For my part, I have a great fear that I may be cast out even from the bridegroom's chamber itself, bound hand and foot, as one who did not prepare wedding garments for himself, but rashly crept into the midst of those reclining [at table]. And indeed — to disclose something of what lies hidden with us — I too was invited by God from boyhood, and was cast upon him from the womb, and from my mother's belly was offered as the gift of my mother's promise; and after this I was confirmed through dangers, and longing for him grew strong in me, and all things converged on this. Hence I too offered myself as a possession to him to whom I had been made over from the cradle and by whom I had been delivered from dangers; I offered him all that was mine. Why do I say all? That which alone I seemed to have: letters and liberal studies, from which I had only this gain, that I might seem to have something to despise and something to which I might prefer Christ. I delighted more in the words of God, and his sayings became to me like a honeycomb, and I called upon prudence and gave my voice to wisdom. But I did not neglect the other things either, that is, to restrain anger, to bridle the tongue, to keep the eye more modest, to govern the belly more strictly, to trample on human glory. But I speak as one foolish, while I do not wish to hide from you that in these things, as far as we could, we made such effort as not to be much inferior to others.

78. But to practise philosophy according to God, and to know how to hold the helm of souls, and to be set over others and rule them, when I myself have not yet learned to obey those who rule rightly — this I judged to be a task beyond me, especially at this time, in which we see men turned this way and that and throwing everything into confusion, so that nothing seems better than to flee from the midst and lie hidden. For the enemy attacks and disturbs everything, and as if in blind darkness stirs up war, so that the members may fight all the more against one another, so that the remnants of charity, if there are any, may be driven out, while new names are acquired for new priests and, as it is written, contempt has been poured out upon princes.

79. All fear has been driven out of [men's] minds, and everywhere shamelessness prevails. Whoever wishes claims for himself the sum of knowledge and reckons the depths of the Spirit to be within himself. And we all wish to be thought learned and catholic on this ground, if we censure others and judge them impious. Sometimes we even choose as judges concerning God those who do not know God, and we throw holy things to dogs and cast pearls before swine, that is, publishing the divine mysteries to polluted ears and minds. This indeed turns out as our enemies wish: though they may not approach our church, yet through us they trample on our holy things. So we have opened to all not the gates of justice but an entrance for slander and disparagement and a road for insolence. And we judge those alone the best, not those who out of the fear of God have not uttered even an idle word from their mouth, but whoever can disparage the brethren most widely and bitterly, or at any rate those who have bitten subtly and by insinuation, and have put toil and pain under their tongue, and the venom of asps has been under their lips.

80. We watch one another carefully, not for our own sins but for others', not to lament them but to charge and reproach [them], nor to heal but to wound further. And we judge the bad and the good not by their character nor by their way of life but by their party; and what pleased [us] in someone today will displease tomorrow if he is of the other party, and he who was praised yesterday will be blamed today. And then the things that are blamed in others are held in admiration among us. We pardon everything easily and gladly in our supporters, even if it is done impiously, so that in evil we may seem kind and magnanimous.

81. All things have become as at the beginning, when the world was not yet arranged in its order and forms, but when all things were confused and disordered and called for the mighty hand and power of the Creator. We are, then, as if in some night battle, using the very faint light of the moon, and that at times darkened by constantly intervening clouds — no recognition of allies and enemies, no distinguishing [them] — or as in a sea fight, when the fury of the winds presses hard and the surge of the waves rises, the thrusts of the poles rebound, the sailors' shouting thunders, the crash of the ships resounds, the groaning of the wounded and the roaring of the very air confound everything, and there is no time for courage nor room for counsel: so we too — wretched me! — rush upon one another and bite and tear one another, so that, of course, we may be consumed by one another.

82. But perhaps the people are like this, but the priest otherwise. No, rather, what was said seems to me now to be fulfilled: the priest has become like the people — which was once said by way of a curse. Or perhaps the lowborn and unskilled crowd is driven by these evils, while all the nobler and more powerful among the people act otherwise. On the contrary, these attack the priests even more openly and strongly. But perhaps, since these too are still men of the world, they do these things for that reason, while our ascetics, who, as they say, are free for God for this very purpose, act more quietly. Yet these wage even open war and a shameless contest against the priests, all the more because, by the appearance of their religious habit, they can more easily be believed by the crowd even when they slander, especially when they raise questions about the faith, which is the sum of things. I do not mean those among whose number I too wish to be, and long to become one of them, who with a sound and healthy purpose take up the contest for the truth, who lay down their necks and their life for the faith of God; for such fighting as makes one near to God is better than that peace which separates from God; for this reason indeed the Holy Spirit bids the warrior be gentle. So I do not speak of warriors of this kind, in whose number I too long to be found.

83. But there are some who stir up huge quarrels from small matters or words, or are roused even by human rather than divine impulses. These enlist as many as possible as allies in their madness, while they put upon their contentiousness and insolence the name of faith, glorious and venerable to all, colouring the cause of their foulest purpose with the appearance of this most honourable word. Because of these, then, as it seems to me, we are both held in hatred among the gentiles and, what is worse, we have no confidence to say that they hate us without cause. And we are also commended very badly to our own people, and especially to those who seem either honourable or religious among the common folk.

84. For when these hear something blameworthy or reprehensible against any of the priests or ministers of God from those who build upon our backs, they take what is charged the more abhorrently, as though for the honour and piety of their own mind, and what they have once believed of one they think of all. And we have become a kind of public theatre, not to angels and men, as Paul, God's athlete, said, who sweated in contests against principalities and powers, but we have become a theatre for all the abject and unworthy and, so to speak, for monsters and beasts, at every time and in every place, in streets, in shops, at banquets, in councils. We are brought even onto the stage itself — which I say with tears — and are mocked by the foulest and most shameless actors, and nothing is now performed so delightfully in mimes, nothing sung so pleasingly in comedies, as the Christian.

85. This has come down on us from this: while we attack one another, while we think ourselves exceedingly catholic, exceedingly faithful, and roused by zeal for God, but not as is fitting, and [think we] contend for God, but not as is right nor as the law of contests prescribes. For our contest has come to this, that we win an infamous victory, so that we lose the palm most when we have won in the contest. Or have we not read that no one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully? Strength alone is not enough for the contestant unless he has also kept the rules of the athletic art. But you, as I see, fight for Christ against Christ. For the name of God is blasphemed among the gentiles through you, as it is written.

86. The demons, indeed, still tremble even now when the name of Christ is invoked, and not even our wickedness has made the strength and power of so great a name vanish; and we do not revere this name but do everything to the injury of so great a name. And whereas we have the command to act so that men, seeing our good works, may glorify our Father who is in heaven, we, turning the force of the precept to the contrary, cause the name of God to be blasphemed among the gentiles through our contentions.

87. And indeed I do not fear wars from outside, nor do I dread that beast which has now risen against the churches — in whom is the fullness of the devil — though he threaten fire, though he brandish swords and beasts, though he prepare crosses and precipices, though he become crueller than all the persecutors who were before him, though he seek out new kinds of torture: I have one remedy against all these, one victory, to have gladly undergone death for Christ.

88. But against this civil war I do not know what to do, what aids to procure for myself, what word of wisdom may help me, what gift of the Spirit I should invoke, with what spiritual arms I should gird myself against the wiles of the devil, what Moses, with hands outstretched on the mountain, already foreshadowing the image of the cross, may restrain these wars, what Joshua, approved leader of the soldiery of God's camp, what David, either playing the lyre or fighting with the sling, and girded by God with strength for war and his fingers trained for battle, what Samuel, stirring heaven with his prayers, drawing down rain, moving the thunder — who will lament and weep over these things worthily?

89. Let some Jeremiah, surely, writing a new lamentation for this new captivity of ours, cry out again to God and say: Spare, Lord, your people, and do not give your inheritance over to reproach, that the gentiles should rule over them. Who will pray to the Lord for us as Noah and Daniel and Job, that this devastation may cease and rest from us for a little, so that at last we may return to ourselves and, as if the mist were driven from our eyes, recognise that we are sons of one father, that we are brothers, so that God's people may no longer be called Judah and Israel, nor Rehoboam and Jeroboam, nor Jerusalem and Samaria, which are now handed over into captivity, now lament at home?

90. And I indeed admit that I am very weak for battles of this kind, and for that reason I confess that I have turned my back. So, veiling my face with confusion, I have sat alone, because I am filled with bitterness. I sought also to be silent, as one who understands that the time is evil, because the beloved have kicked back and have become children who depart. The vine too, glad in its branches, and the true vine, wholly fruitful, has been turned into bitterness, and the diadem of beauty has been changed into disgrace; the seal of my right hand and the crown of my boasting has become confusion to me. But if anyone else is ready boldly and bravely to undergo the contests of battles of this kind, him I both call blessed for his confidence and rank above myself.

91. I do not yet make mention of those wars by which we are attacked within ourselves by our own vices and passions, and are pressed day and night by the fiery goads of this body of humiliation and body of death, while the enticements of visible things provoke and incite us everywhere, now secretly, now even openly; while this mud of dregs, to which we cling, breathes out the stench of its filth through wider veins; and while the law of sin, which is in our members, fights against the law of the spirit, as it strives to lead captive the royal image which is within us, so that whatever has flowed into us by the benefit of that divine and first creation may yield as its spoils. Hence scarcely anyone, perhaps, governing himself by a long and strict philosophy and gradually recalling the nobility of his soul, may recall and turn back to God the nature of light that is in him, joined to this lowly and dark mud; or if indeed he acts with God's favour, he will recall both alike, provided that by long and constant meditation he grows used always to look upward, and with tighter reins to lift up the matter bound to him, which drags him badly downward and weighs him down. But before he attains this, and before he surpasses other men in purity of heart, as far as can be, he ought not to wish to be set over those than whom he does not feel himself to be more purified, nor think it safe to become mediator of the people before God — which is the special office of the priest — unless he sees himself near to God and a friend of God.

92. But I ought to show you how I came into this fear, lest perhaps you think me more timid than is right, so that you may judge me not so much fearful as taking counsel for myself. When God spoke to Moses on the mountain, he ordered many others also to go up with him, among whom were Aaron with his sons the priests and seventy presbyters from the elders; all of these were ordered to stand at a distance and worship, but Moses alone is ordered to come near, and no one else to go up with him. From this it is plainly shown that it is not for just anyone to come near to God, unless one is such as Moses, who could receive the glory of God in himself. And earlier too, when the giving of the law was first being prepared, the sound of trumpets and lightning and thunder resounded about the rest, and the darkness and smoke of the burning mountain, and fear and dreadful terror, so that even a beast, if it touched the mountain, was stoned — and so for them, standing far off, it was a great thing even to hear the sound of the voice, and that when they had been sanctified with all diligence and caution — but Moses alone both climbs the mountain and enters the cloud, and is nowhere scorched by the blazing flames, and receives the tablets: for the mass of the common people, tablets of the letter, but for those who grasp the things of the spirit, tablets written by the Spirit of the living God.

93. But Nadab and Abihu, because they had offered strange fire for the incense of the altar, are consumed by fire for this alone, and had almost the same place of punishment and death as of fault and impiety. And not even Aaron was fit to intercede, though he was certainly their father and, second after Moses, drew near to God in the honour of the priesthood. Eli the priest too is condemned for the iniquity of his sons, because he punished them with too little severity when they profaned the divine sacrifices. [...] he did indeed restrain them and did indeed rebuke them, but with the leniency and gentleness of a father, not with the severity and authority of a high priest. What of that Uzzah, who, when the heifer, impatient of its burden, had turned aside from the track of the straight path, held up with diligent and anxious hand the ark of the Lord's covenant as it was on the very point of falling — was he not punished with death by God solely because he had touched holy things?

94. I know that not even bodily blemishes in priests are passed over, but everything is examined and required by the law, that neither victim nor priest should have any bodily defect. These are surely figures of that perfection and purity which ought to be in the heart and soul of the priest. And not even the priestly garments themselves or the vessels of the ministry is it lawful for just anyone even to touch or handle. The sacrifices themselves too are permitted to be eaten not by all indiscriminately but only by certain persons, and within a fixed time and within a prescribed place. Nor is it lawful for anyone even to imitate the composition of the oil of chrism, or the mixture of the incense. And what more shall I say? Not even the temple itself may be entered by one who is not clean in soul and body even in the smallest things. And how rashly and thoughtlessly we rush into the very holy of holies, which only the one high priest might enter, and he once a year, who alone was permitted to go beyond the inner veil and see the ark of the covenant and the mercy-seat and the Cherubim — which now everyone thinks it lawful for himself both to see and to touch!

95. Knowing these things, then, and since no one is worthy to be either a priest or a sacrifice of the most high God who has not first presented himself as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, and performed his reasonable service, and offered to God the sacrifice of praise and a contrite spirit, the only sacrifice God seeks, all others being rejected and despised, how could I dare to approach the priesthood, and the offering of sacrifices, and the celebration of the image and figure of the heavenly sacraments? Or how [could I dare] to take up the priestly dress and name, I who did not first know that I had perfected my hands with holy works, who had not yet taught my eye to look rightly on the creation of God, who had not first opened my ear to the instruction of the Lord, so that I might deserve to be given an ear that would not be hard of hearing, and that there might be a precious sardius as an earring in my ear, which is the word of the wise in an obedient ear? I who did not first open my mouth and draw in the spirit, or open my mouth wide, that it might be filled with the spirit for speaking out the mysteries and doctrines of piety? Who did not offer my tongue, that it might be loosed in due season and filled with exultation in the psalms and songs of the Lord, rising up like a morning plectrum on the psaltery and harp, rising at dawn and crying to the Lord until my throat becomes hoarse and my tongue cleaves to my throat? Before my feet stand upon the rock and are made perfect like a deer's, so that my steps may be directed according to God, so that my footsteps may not grow weak or come near to slipping? Before all my members become weapons of righteousness, and all mortality in me is swallowed up by life, and the flesh is subject to the spirit?

96–99. Who would dare to approach this rank before his heart and mind are kindled by the pure words of the Lord, tried by fire, while [the Lord] opens the scriptures to him? Before he writes them down threefold in the breadth of his heart, so as to have the mind of Christ? Before he is found worthy to enter the treasures of knowledge, hidden from others, invisible and obscure, so that, having received riches from them, he may himself enrich others too, comparing spiritual things with spiritual? Before he contemplates, as it is fitting to contemplate, the delight of the Lord, and visits his temple, or rather himself becomes the temple of the living God and the dwelling-place of Christ in the spirit? Before he recognises the distinction and the kinship between figure and truth, so that he may know more carefully what he ought to withdraw from and what he ought to hold to, since the truth holds and the shadow passes away, and so that he may wholly escape from the oldness of the letter and serve in the newness of the spirit, and pass over entirely from the law to grace, which is fulfilled spiritually in the destruction of the body? Before he runs through all the titles and powers of Christ, by works and by knowledge, both those which are highest and those which, for our sake, are his lower and last? That is, to know that he is God and that he is Son of God, and to know also in what way he is [so]: that he is image, that he is Word, that he is wisdom, that he is truth, that he is light, that he is life, that he is power, that he is vapour, that he is emanation, that he is radiance, that he is creator, that he is king, that he is head, that he is law, that he is way, that he is door, that he is foundation, that he is rock, that he is pearl, that he is peace, that he is righteousness, that he is sanctification, that he is redemption, that he is man, that he is servant, that he is shepherd, that he is lamb, that he is priest, that he is victim, that he is firstborn of all creation, that he is firstborn from the dead, that he is resurrection. Who would dare, before he becomes a sharer in all these names in reality and in deed, before he shares with Christ in each of them by fulfilling them in himself and becomes his partaker in each of them, before he has leisure and learns to speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, before, having become a man, he puts away the things of a child and is now counted in the number of Israel and in the army of God, before he can take up the cross of Christ and follow him and lose his life for his sake, so as to find it in eternal life and be brought to the fullness of Christ — how can anyone dare to approach the rank of teacher and teach things which he does not yet feel fulfilled in himself?

100. I said within myself: let others sail, and in hope of great gains undergo the dangers of the sea; to me it is more pleasing to stand on solid ground and seek the blade of grain in the furrows of a little plot, and to lead a meagre life in poverty, than to seek foreign riches amid the perils of the waves.

101. For the stronger and the able it is indeed a loss not to administer greater offices nor to exercise their virtue towards very many, but to be confined in small and modest matters, as if someone were to light the space of a small room with a huge lamp, or wished to fit powerful, manly armour on a small body and boyish limbs; but for the small it is safer to lift a small load and not beyond their strength, lest they both become a laughing-stock and at the same time incur danger, just as it is fitting for no one to build even a tower except one who also has the means of completing it ready to hand.

102–103. This is the defence and excuse for my flight, and these are the reasons that had separated or drawn me away from you, O brothers and dearest friends; for such thoughts then pressed me hard to withdraw further. But what called me back was, first, longing for you, and still more the fact that I was longed for than that I longed. For nothing is so strong for love as when affection exists on both sides. Second, my greatest care and chief concern, the venerable grey hairs of my holy parents, who were labouring more on my account than from old age itself: the honour of this Abrahamic head and its angelic appearance, and the due reverence for my mother Sarah, who also bore us spiritually in the faith of the gospel, to whom it was necessary that I should be a staff of old age. Out of regard for them, and to pay them the due duties of filial piety, I even disregarded the pursuit of philosophy, which I held precious and dear above all possessions and affections. In which, to speak more truly, I practised philosophy in this very thing, that I should not seem to practise philosophy. I did not, then, endure that all these things should be poured away and abolished for me under the pretext of a single occasion, nor that the paternal blessings should be taken from me, which one of the ancient saints is reported even to have stolen by craft, deceiving his father with food and hairy skins. These, then, are the two reasons to which I chiefly yielded, and which were able most of all to soften my resolve. And I think that neither of them seems unworthy for that swelling of my thoughts to have yielded to, since there is indeed a time also to be overcome, just as there is a time for every thing. And perhaps it is sometimes better to be overcome well than to overcome badly.

104–105. The third, however, is what most of all and above all subdued and subjected me. When I have set it out, I will say no more of the rest. I remembered the days of old, and in matters so great, so difficult and so arduous I did not dare to trust my own counsels sufficiently, but sought a judgement on what to do from the authority of holy men, and set the examples of the ancients as a rule for present affairs. For these things were not written for us superfluously, nor so that, in the manner of the Greeks, we might be educated by them or delighted in words. That is what usually happens in their fables or histories, that the charm of a composed poem and the very sweetness of narration entice minds and delight the hearing; our writings, in which not one iota or stroke is idle, in all that they either relate as done or prescribe as to be done, lay down the principles and rules of our life, so that if ever the need to deliberate finds us in doubtful matters, we may return to the examples of our forebears and learn from them what we should choose and what we should avoid.

106. What history, then, did I remember, and from what did the occasion of this counsel arise for me? I will tell it briefly, and you listen patiently. Jonah once fled from the face of God, or rather thought he was fleeing. But he was caught by the pursuit of the sea, by the storm, by the lot, by the belly of the whale, and by a burial of three days and nights foreshadowing the form of a future mystery. And he fled lest he should either be the minister of sad news to the Ninevites or afterwards be found a liar, if the city were saved through repentance; for he did not begrudge them their salvation, but declined the ministry of falsehood, deferring in all things to the prophetic dignity, which he saw would in a sense be disfigured in him if it were defamed with the stain of falsehood, since the ignorant and unskilled crowd cannot understand or foresee the profound knowledge of the future dispensation.

107–109. But I heard a certain very wise man expounding these things and giving an account of this history, which seems as it were absurd, in such a way that he would not even admit this as the cause of blessed Jonah's flight, that he went down to Joppa and from Joppa fled to Tarshish, as if, he said, he believed that God did not know what he was doing, or as if this were to flee from the face of God, to give himself to the sea and the waves. I will not say that this belongs to prophetic knowledge, to which even deep things become known and obscure things are lit up, but I do not think it belongs even to any man, however ignorant and unskilled; on the contrary, whoever has gone on the sea says that then above all he has committed his safety into the hands of God. Jonah, then, was not unaware that the most mighty hand of God is present on the sea too and is at hand everywhere, the hand which he was being sent to preach to others as well, nor did he presume that he could escape the power of the Godhead anywhere (this is not to be believed); but because he foresaw that through this ministry of his the Spirit was prefiguring that, his people Israel being spurned and cast off, the gift of prophetic grace would be transferred to the Gentiles, he therefore evaded the duty of preaching, so as not to render the sad service of the casting off of his ancestral nation. Then, having left the place which is 'the contemplation of joy' (for so Joppa is interpreted in the language of the Hebrews), having left, then, 'the contemplation of joy', that is, of that ancient magnificence and dignity, he gave himself to a sea of grief and sadness. Hence the storm, hence the sleep, hence the shipwreck; hence he is roused and has the lot cast on him, and confesses his flight, and is thrown overboard, and is received by the whale and is not consumed, but there calls upon God, and, standing for Christ before Christ, after the third day he rises again in Christ. But let the discussion of these things wait for us a little, so that afterwards, if God grants, it may be explained more fully and carefully.

110. Now, however, let us pursue the point to which our discourse had been directed, since he perhaps had some pardon for deferring the prophetic duty on account of the cause we have mentioned; but for me what excuse will suffice, what cause will come to my aid, what room for making amends will be left if I resist any longer? And I do not know whether I should call it heavy or light, the yoke of the priesthood, however it was laid on me, if I refuse it too stubbornly.

111. For if this, which alone among all our excuses we hold as the stronger, be granted to us, that we are far inferior to what would suffice for discharging the priesthood, yet what shall we do about the fact that on the other side we incur the more ruinous charge of disobedience? And perhaps the danger from contempt will be graver for us than we think the danger from rashness to be, since for one who sins in this direction there remains no further room for amending or correcting.

112. Placed, then, between these two fears, of ascending and of descending, and weighing myself on either side in an even balance, and inclining now to this side, now to that, as if driven by winds, at last I yielded to the one that weighed more heavily, the fear of disobedience, which, having driven off the other as being stronger and more vehement, claimed me wholly for itself and held me. Consider, then, whether we rightly and justly balance ourselves between these fears, while we neither take up honours not granted nor refuse those that have been conferred, since in the one case impudence is condemned, in the other disobedience, and both are a fault of inexperience. We wish, then, to walk a middle way between the too timid and the too rash, so as to be more modest than those who strive for undue honours with foul ambition, and a little more confident than those who, from fear of the judgement to come, shrink even from all good actions.

113. Deliberating thus, then, on such matters, and measuring each thing by its own weight, I added this also to give my mind confidence: that the faith of obedience may earn some reward from God, and that what is lacking may be filled up while what is present is wholly trusted, so that faith may make perfect the one whom fear held imperfect. For we read it written that he who fears is not perfect in love; but perfect love casts out fear. On the other hand I saw that no aids come to the help of the danger of disobedience and unbelief. Nor do I find anything that would give confidence to one who distrusts; on the contrary, I fear that on behalf of those entrusted to us we may have to hear this: I will require their soul at your hands; and: As you have spurned me, that you should not be leaders and princes of my people, so I too will spurn you, that none of you shall be made king; and: As you did not hear my voice, but turned a hard back and were disobedient, so it shall be when you call upon me, but I will not look upon your prayer nor hear you. May it not befall us to hear such answers from the just Judge, nor may that voice come to us from him to whom, though we sing of mercy, we shall also sing of judgement together with it.

114. But again we turn back to the histories of the ancients and the deeds of the noble men of old. Among them we see that some, when they were appointed to rule peoples or were called by the grace of God to the prophetic office, yielded most readily when invited, while others for some time put off the grace of the one inviting. Yet we do not see either group blamed, nor the ready swiftness of obedience censured in the one, nor the circumspect hesitation of fear in the other, since the latter revered the greatness of the ministry, while to the former faith gave confidence, being sure that all things are possible to him who believes. Aaron was ready, but Moses had resisted much; Isaiah readily obeys, but Jeremiah dreaded his youthful age, and did not take up the ministry of prophecy before he received from God a promise of strength and steadfastness.

115. By these thoughts I was restored again, and softened by counsels of this kind in constant wrestling, and, like iron laid on the anvil, I was softened and tamed by the blows, as it were, of hammers. There came besides, to ripen my counsel, time too, which softens and digests all things. Above all, however, that which is written: My counsels are your ordinances, to which I have entrusted my whole life. Therefore I do not resist nor speak against it, says my Lord, who was not called to the leadership of a people, but was led like a sheep to the slaughter. I prostrate myself, then, and fall down and submit myself to the most mighty hand of God, and ask pardon for the past time of withdrawal and delay, if perhaps any guilt arises for me from this. I have been silent, but I shall not always be silent. I withdrew for a little time, to examine and visit myself, and so that some consolation for my sadness might arise. But now I have come to exalt the Lord in the churches and to praise him in the seat of the elders. If that was blameworthy, this earns pardon.

116. But what need is there now of longer words? You have us now, O shepherds and fellow shepherds; you possess us, O most holy and most worthy flock of Christ; you possess us, father, overcome in all things and yielding in all things, subject to you more by the laws of Christ than by those of nature. See, you now have our submission; give in return your blessing. Guide us by your prayers, instruct us by your word, strengthen us by the Spirit; for the blessing of the father strengthens the houses of the sons. And may I be strengthened, as well as this spiritual house, in which is my rest for ever and ever, in which I will dwell, because I have chosen it, so that from this church and from this house we may together be found worthy to be transferred to the church of the firstborn, which is enrolled in the heavens.

117. This, then, is our apology before you, and this the close of our discourse. And may the God of peace, who made both one and restored us to one another, who makes the mighty sit upon thrones and who raises the needy from the earth and lifts up the poor from the dunghill; who chose David his servant and took him from the flocks of sheep, though he was the last and youngest among the sons of Jesse; who gives the word to those who preach the gospel with great power for the perfecting of their preaching — may he, holding our right hand, guide us in his will and receive us with glory. May he himself rule the rulers, himself guide the guides, so that we may feed his flock with discipline and not with the implements of an unskilled shepherd; may he himself grant strength and fortitude to his people, and present to himself a clean and white flock, spotless in all things and worthy of the heavenly folds, where is the dwelling of those who rejoice in the splendours of the saints, so that in his temple we may all speak of glory, flock and shepherds together, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory for ever and ever.
