VII. On the Reconciliation and Unity of the Monks.

1. Eagerness has loosened our tongue, and we disregard the law of men for the sake of the law of the Holy Spirit; we yield to no one, but now bring forth words of peace. Before this, while the members were fighting against one another, while the holy and venerable body of Christ was being divided and torn into parts, when our bones were almost scattered beside the underworld, and as the thick soil of the earth is broken up by a cruel plough and cut with deeper furrows, when the enemy, rending and tearing the undivided and unsplittable tunic of Christ, which had been woven from the top throughout, had succeeded in doing this through us, the ministers, which he could not do through those who had crucified Christ: when, I say, things were so, then I set a guard on my mouth and gave silence to my lips, since I saw that it follows that the mind ought first to be purified by the practice of philosophy, and only then to open the mouth and draw in the Spirit and utter a good word and speak the wisdom of God perfectly among the perfect; for this seems to me to be the order of spiritual speech. For, according to the judgement of the most wise Solomon, for everything [there is] a time. For this sacrifice above all God requires of us: purity and a contrite heart [is a sacrifice to God] and the sacrifice of praise. For he wants us to be a new creation in Christ and a new man, and whatever else of this kind divine Scripture relates. The first wisdom, then, is to despise and disdain that wisdom which lies in words and in arguments, or in cleverness of speech, or which relies on captious syllogisms and empty contradictions. But I would rather speak five words in the church with my understanding, so as to instruct others also, than many thousands of words in a tongue and with such a sound of the trumpet as does not give a clear sound to prepare my soldier for spiritual war. This wisdom, then, I praise and this I embrace, through which the lowly have become glorious and through which the outcast have come to honour, and in which fishermen enclosed the whole world in the nets of the gospel, overcoming with a word completed and cut short the wisdom that is being destroyed. For not he who is wise in word seems wise to me, nor he who produces a polished and fluent tongue but remains unskilled in soul, like those tombs which outwardly appear whitewashed and adorned to men but inwardly are full of uncleanness and stench; but he seems wise to me who admonishes and speaks out a little about virtue of soul, but shows more in his actions and works, and confirms the credibility of his word by the testimony of his works; for no one could love beauty of form painted in a picture as much as [beauty] residing in a body, nor were riches seen in dreams as useful as those held in the hands. So too that wisdom is illustrious, not which flies about in words but which consists in virtues. So indeed Scripture also says that a good understanding is to all who do it, not to those who speak and proclaim it. Of this wisdom, then, time reveals the firmer proofs, which in old men is truly a crown of glorying. For if a man ought not to be called blessed before death, as Solomon thinks, and I too, because it is uncertain what the time to come may bring forth, since the life of men is very changeable while this body of lowliness is always turned and changed this way and that, how is he who has already passed most of this life blamelessly and, escaping the uncertain sea of our dwelling, hopes now to see the harbour and at any moment to enter it, not much safer and more blessed than one for whom much of the danger of the sea still remains?

4. Do not, then, close the tongue which has taught many good things, whose fruits are many and whose offspring of righteousness are without number; how many are its children and how many its treasures, lift up your eyes round about and see. This whole people is the one you have begotten in Christ Jesus through the gospel. Do not, then, now begrudge the grace of a good word, even if it be brief. You know how to say much briefly. And if not, at least cry out with that spiritual voice which God heard even when Moses was silent, saying to him: Why do you cry to me? — that is, when he was entreating him in the spirit. Order and prepare the people for me, your sheep and nursling, and after that also your shepherd, and now indeed high priest together with you. Teach me also something of pastoral discipline, and this people about obedience; at least philosophise to us something about this present blow and devastation: about the most just judgements of God, whether we comprehend them or are ignorant of the great abyss, and how his mercy too is a balance, according to holy Isaiah. For his goodness is not without judgement, even if it did not seem fair to those who had laboured in the vineyard all day that they had been made equal with the later ones. But wrath too, according to the measure of sins, is called a cup in the hand of the Lord and a draught of ruin; when it is drunk, something seems to be taken away and vomited out of the crimes of those who drink, and again unmixed wrath is tempered by clemency. For he inclines from what is unmixed and violent to what is milder and more moderate, namely for those who are corrected by fear, and who from small tribulations conceive and bring forth conversion and beget the spirit of salvation full and whole. Yet he keeps back its dregs, which is the last and final part of wrath, to pour it all out upon those who refuse to be healed by admonitions and rebukes, but rather are hardened the more by gentleness, after the manner of the most hardened Pharaoh, who was kept back for the impious as an example of the power of God.

5. Tell us, then: whence these blows, and whence the scourges, and what is their reason? Is the motion of the universe itself driven at random and by chance and without any helm, and do these things happen by accident as if with no ruler, as it seems to those who are foolishly wise; or by some reason and order, and, just as all things were made and composed and set in order from the beginning, so too now is the world moved and governed, as only he knows who moves it and controls it with the eternal reins of providence? Whence, then, barrenness? Whence the corruption of the air? Whence hailstorms, and this present blow and devastation and chastisement of ours? Whence plagues and diseases? Whence earthquakes and terrors of the sea and from heaven? Or how is the earth, which was formed by the creator for the service of men, and whose goods we all ought to enjoy equally, turned to the punishment of the impious, so that in the very things granted and allowed to us, for which we have been ungrateful, we pay the penalty, and come to know through punishments the power of those things whose grace we did not recognise from benefits? How is it that to some sins are repaid double from the hand of the Lord and a twofold measure of wickedness is returned, while for others, when they are chastised, the vengeance for sins is said to be poured sevenfold into their bosom? Or what is that saying, that the measure of the Amorites was not yet full in crimes? How, then, is the sinner left alone and the righteous punished, or again the sinner punished and the righteous left alone and kept safe, and now remedy is applied already here, now everything is reserved for there? What, then, are these blows, or whence? Are they proofs of virtue or punishment of wickedness? And whether it is better to be humbled as those placed under punishment, or to disregard and neglect [them] as brought on for the sake of testing — teach us these things, admonish us about them, so that we may neither bear this present blow too heavily, nor again, descending into the depth of evils, despise [it] — for this vice too exists among men — but that we may be humbled under the chastisement of the Lord, lest, while we neglect and despise this, we provoke a greater wrath of God against us.

6. Grievous is the barrenness of the earth, grievous the devastation of the crops — for who denies it? — especially when the joy of them was in hope and when the grain was already near the very granaries. Grievous it is that the harvest has been carried off unripe, and the weeping farmers look down on their flattened crops and sit as if beside the dead bodies of their dear ones; [crops] which the gentle rain made grow, but the stormy and cruel [rain] cut down. From them the reaper has not filled his hand, nor he who gathers sheaves his bosom, nor have the passers-by said to the reapers: The blessing of the Lord be upon you. A pitiable spectacle has occurred: the earth itself lies defaced, the tresses in which it rejoiced torn and plucked away, and made ugly from its very adornment. Blessed Joel too mourns it, lamenting the calamity of famine with mighty tragic laments. And another prophet, comparing the final devastation with the former fertility and speaking of the wrath of God laying waste the land, says: What is before it is a paradise of delights, and what is behind it a plain of destruction. Grievous, I say, are these things, and very grievous, so long as we think only of these present things and do not yet conceive fear of graver ones, since in bodily pains too what presses at the present always seems graver than all that does not bring present torment. Far more violent and grievous are the things which the treasuries of the wrath of God keep in store, which may we never experience. And we will not experience them, if we fly to the mercy of God and incline to us by tears him who wills mercy rather than death, so that we may turn away by our conversion what remains of the wrath of God; since this is still the gentleness and clemency of God and mild chastisement, and certain beginnings of correction applied as to those still little and nursing. This is still a kind of smoke of wrath and the omens of punishments, not yet burning fire, not yet devouring flame nor kindled coals. This is a threat and a menace, and while little has come forth, the greater and strong things are held back, so that in striking he may correct, but in threatening may amend the more, making a way for his wrath; and in his immense goodness he begins with the lesser, so that we may not need the greater and graver. These he will surely apply as well, if we provoke them by despising these lesser ones.

7. I know the brandished sword and the sword made drunk in heaven, slaying and spurning and bereaving, which is commanded not to spare even to the flesh and the marrow. I know him who, though he is impassible, comes to meet [us] like a ravening she-bear, and like a leopard on the road of the Assyrians, not only for those who were [Assyrians] then, but also for every one who is now an Assyrian in wickedness. I know that no one can escape the strength and swiftness of his wrath, when he has awakened over our impieties and when zeal pursues his enemies, the zeal which consumes the adversaries. I know the shaking off and the striking back, and the burning of the heart and the dismay of the mind and the loosening of the knees, and very many other punishments of the impious of this kind. For I pass over speaking of those judgements to which he hands us on and delivers us, after much pardon has been granted here, so that it is better for us to be chastised and purged [here] than to be sent on to those punishments, where it is the time of penalties rather than of purgings. For just as he who is mindful of God here is not in death, as blessed David declares, so those who are in hell do not have the correction of confession, since indeed in the present life the power is granted us to do what we will, but there [we must] render an account of our deeds.

8. What then shall we do on that day, about which one of the prophets terrifies [us] most violently, when he says that God will judge with us on the mountains and hills, and will sit in session against us and dispute, and set our sins before our face — accusers, that is, most bitter — and will also bring forward all his benefits which he has bestowed on us and compare [them] with our crimes, and match thoughts with thoughts and convict deeds by deeds, when, seeking from us the dignity of the pure image, he finds it effaced and darkened, when at the last each one, marked out by his own verdict, will surely be condemned?

9. Who then will be an advocate there? What intercession? What fabrications? What arts? What forensic cunning will be brought forward against the truth? By what rewards will the judgement be corrupted? All things will hang in the balance of justice: our deeds and words and thoughts, evil and good, will be weighed against one another in opposite pans, so that the side which outweighs may prevail, and where the work tips, there the sentence may fall. No other will, no other judgement, no excuse through second works will be sought any longer, nor will there be time for borrowing oil from the wise virgins or buying [it] from those who sell, when the lamps are going out. Nor is there place for the repentance of the rich man burning in the flame and seeking the amendment of his kinsmen. So there will no longer be time for any delay, but only the last and terrible judgement — or rather just, and therefore the more terrible because just. For then the thrones will be set and the Ancient of Days will sit, and the books will be opened and the river of fire will flow, and light will go before and darkness will be prepared; and those who have done good will go forth to the resurrection of life, which is now hidden in Christ and will afterwards be manifested with him, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgement, in which those who did not believe have already been condemned by the Word of God judging. Some, then, that ineffable and immeasurable light will receive, that is, the splendour and knowledge and clearer illumination of the holy and blessed Trinity. It mingles pure and spotless with pure and spotless minds, which I hold alone and above all to be the kingdom of heaven; but for those who are unworthy, along with all the rest, there will also be this, the greatest punishment of all, that they are cast away from God, and the very shame and confusion of conscience, of which there is no end and no remedy anywhere. But of these things later.

10. But now what shall we do, brothers, crushed and humbled and made drunk, not with wine nor strong drink, by which men are a little moved and troubled, but made drunk by the force of the blow which the Lord has brought on, saying: 'And you, be moved and troubled', he who has given the despisers the spirit of sorrow and compunction to drink, to whom it is also said: 'Behold, you despisers, and look and marvel at the marvels, and perish'? How shall we endure his rebukes, or what answer shall we give, when, on top of the multitude of his benefits which we received ungratefully, he begins also to charge to us his chastisements and to count up the remedies and medicines, which were applied and yet we were not healed? And he calls [us] sons indeed, but defiled; or sons, but strangers, and limping from his paths, while they walk in strange and rough ways. So he says: 'What ought I to have done for you and did not do? By what ought I to have corrected you and did not correct [you]? I used gentler remedies. I passed over the scourges of the Egyptians, the blood drunk from rivers and springs and all the waters turned to gore. That first plague of theirs I left aside. I passed over also the frogs and the gnats and the dog-fly and the other scourges. I began with oxen and beasts of burden and flocks; I turned the fifth plague upon the dumb animals, sparing men. That affliction has not yet touched you, but you have become more brutish to me even than the dumb animals. For, as I see, this chastisement does nothing for amendment. I withheld the rains from you: one part received the shower, and the part on which I did not rain withered. And you said: We will hold out and act manfully. Therefore I brought hail upon you and mowed down your vineyards and your orchards and your crops; yet your wickedness I could not cut off, and now I have recognised that you are hard and your neck is a sinew of iron.'

11. This, I think, is what the Lord would say to us, if we are not amended by his scourges, since indeed the despiser remains in his contempt and the unjust persists in injustice. Nor does the chastisement brought from heaven achieve anything in us; the scourges do no good. 'The iron bellows has already failed in the furnace, the lead has failed, the silversmith works in vain: your wickednesses are not consumed. I reckoned this to you long ago through Jeremiah; now then, do you provoke me?' says the Lord. 'Or is my hand not strong enough to bring other plagues and other torments as well? I still have the burning eruptions of boils, which were produced through Moses when the ash and embers were lifted into the air, he who at that time was the minister of God's indignation for chastising Egypt. There is still the locust, there is the darkness that can be felt, there is still the last plague, the destruction of the firstborn, which no one escaped, nor could anyone evade the hand of the destroyer except him alone who smeared his doorposts with the blood of the lamb, that is, who sealed his faith and works with the blood of Christ and the ordinances of the new covenant, who was crucified together with Christ, who was buried with him and rose with him, so that he may also be glorified together with him, both now and at his last coming.'

12. But far be it from us that, along with the other chastisements, the good and merciful God should charge this one also to us, saying: 'Since you walked perversely with me, I too will walk with you in perverse fury'; or again: 'I struck you with blight and with mildew and with [...], and I gained nothing. Outside, the sword made you childless, and not even so did you turn to me, says the Lord.' May it not befall that it be said of us that we were made a vineyard for the beloved, and were planted and propped up with stakes and surrounded with a wall and waited for, that we should bear grapes, but we bore thorns, and not justice but an outcry, so that it became necessary for the wall to be destroyed and for us to be trampled, and for the tower to be overthrown and for us to become plunder, so that we be no longer pruned nor dug, and moreover — which is most unhappy of all — that the clouds be commanded not to rain rain upon us. I, brothers, am driven by such thoughts in adversity, and console myself with these admonitions; thus I know how to think about the chastisements of the Lord, and when I turn over counsels of this kind within myself, I turn again to prayer and supplication of the Lord, and I add to what we said above and say together with you: if you follow me and join your minds and thoughts with me, let us say together: We have sinned, we have acted unjustly, we have committed impiety, for we have forgotten your commandments and have walked after the thoughts of our most evil heart, and we have not walked worthily of the calling with which you called us through the gospel of your Christ, nor have we received his holy sufferings fittingly, nor have we accepted his humiliation as it deserved, but we have become a reproach to your beloved. Priest and people, we have gone out of our minds; we have all turned aside together, together we have become unprofitable; there is none who does judgement and justice, there is not even one. We have shut out your mercies and your clemency from us, and we have turned away the bowels of your compassion through our malice and the wickedness of our most evil devising. You, Lord, have shown goodness and mercy to us, but we iniquity. You are patient and of great mercy, but we are hard and deserving of many scourges. We know your goodness, though we are unbelieving. According to what we have sinned we have as yet been chastised little. You are terrible, and who will withstand you? Trembling will seize the mountains before you, and who will withstand the greatness of your arm? And if you loose the floodgates of heaven, who will shut them? It is light in your eyes to make poor and rich, to give life and to hand over to death, to strike and to heal, since the very thing you will is a finished work. 'You', said one of the ancients who made supplication to you, 'were angry, and we sinned.' But for us it is time to say the reverse: We sinned, and you were angry. And therefore we have become a reproach to our neighbours. You turned your face away from us, and our countenance was filled with shame. But spare, Lord! Spare, Lord! Be merciful, Lord! Do not hand us over to the end because of our iniquities, nor make us an example for the chastisement of others. Rather, Lord, correct and amend us by the punishments of others — of those nations, we mean, which have not known your name and have not been subject to your power; but we are your people and the rod of your inheritance and the sheep of your pasture. Therefore chastise us, Lord, yet in mercy and not in wrath, lest you make us few, Lord, beyond all who dwell on the earth.

13. With these words and these prayers I call upon and invite the mercy of the Lord. And if I could offer myself as a whole burnt offering, a sacrifice, to soften the Lord's wrath, I would not spare [myself], I would not delay. But you too, O devout people, you also must imitate your fearful and timid priest. I beg you, my children, I beseech you, join your lamentation to mine and mingle your weeping with my weeping; and let us call forth the Lord's clemency by an abundance of tears, and with weeping put out the fire kindled by the divine indignation; let us soften the Lord's wrath by our conversion. Let us sanctify a fast, let us proclaim a healing. For these are the remedies the holy prophets suggest to us. Let us gather the elders, let us tear the nursing infants from their mothers' very breasts and lay them before the face of the Lord, an age worthy of all pity, and the only one that may deserve to win God's mercy by its wailing. We priests and ministers of the Lord, too, are admonished by those same prophetic words to go about in ash and sackcloth and to lament night and day between the steps of the altar in a pitiable garb, crying out and calling to the Lord with a tearful voice, and, both for ourselves and for the people, to leave out absolutely nothing, whether of labour or of speech, by which God is believed able to be reconciled. So we too cry out, together with you and for you: Spare, Lord, your people, and do not give your inheritance over to reproach, for we have as much more of tribulation as we have of honour. Learn from us, then, little children, compunction before the Lord, since we are afflicted for you, and offer your amendment together with us, so that we may deserve to obtain pardon of the impending plague.

14. Come then, all, let us worship and fall down before him and weep in the sight of the Lord who made us. Let us order a common mourning; every age and sex, each in its own rank, let us raise a voice of lamentation, and in place of those voices of injustice which we uttered before, let us now send forth a voice of weeping and lamentation into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth. Let us forestall his anger by confession. Who knows whether perhaps the Lord will turn and repent and leave mercies behind him? I, however, know that he will do it; I promise, on the strength of the Lord's clemency, that as soon as we have turned, he too will cease to be angry — which he does indeed against his nature — and will turn to mercies — which he does indeed in accordance with his nature —: for to the former he is driven by us, but the latter is in him by nature. Only let us take pity on ourselves and open the way for his just mercies. Let us sow in tears, that we may reap in joy. Let us become Ninevites and not Sodomites. Let us quickly heal our evils, lest we be consumed in evils. Let us hear the preaching of Jonah, lest we be burned up with fire and sulphur; or if we must indeed flee from Sodom, let us climb the mountain or take refuge in Zoar and enter it with the rising sun. Let us not stand still in all the region nor look back behind us, lest we become a little pillar of salt, an undying memorial of sin.

15. Let us know that never to sin at all is beyond man and belongs to God alone; of the angels I say nothing, lest we open a road to vices and unbar an entrance to malicious contradictions. Not to sin, then, belongs to God, but incurable sin belongs to the devil and to all who serve under him. But for those who sin to turn from sin belongs to men who believe in God and whose portion is among those who are saved. For although this earth also wraps within itself no little wickedness, and the earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that thinks many things and looks upward — indeed is created for this, to seek the things that are above — yet the image of God should cleanse away the stain of the bodily flood and lift up the flesh joined to it on the wings of the word of God. And although it would have been better not even to need cleansing of this kind, but to have remained in that first dignity, to which we also hasten back after the present amendment, and it would have been better not to fall away from the tree of life through the most bitter taste of sin, yet in the second place it is more profitable to be amended and corrected after a fall than to remain in wickedness. For whom the Lord loves he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives. And again it says: The soul that is not chastised is incurable. It is grievous, then, to be struck by a plague, but it is much more grievous not to be amended when chastised, as one of the prophets says of Israel: Lord, you scourged them and they felt no pain; you chastised them and they would not accept discipline; and again: And the people was not converted until it was struck; and: Why is it that my people has turned away with a most evil turning away? From which it will be crushed and destroyed to the very last.

16. But this too is terrible, to fall into the hands of the living God, and what was said: But the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth. For nothing escapes the hearing of God, since he heard even the voice of Abel's blood. For where could anyone hide from God, when God fills all things and is everywhere? Where will anyone flee from the face of God? If someone is lifted up to heaven on wings, he will be there; if into the underworld, he will nowhere be absent; if to the east, if one goes down into the depth of the sea, nowhere will he avoid that great eye. This [eye] the prophet Nahum also dreads, when he brought forth the burden of the word of God against Nineveh and described God as jealous, avenging with fury upon his adversaries and using such severity that no room was left even for a second vengeance against the wicked. And when I hear Isaiah too accusing the people of Sodom and the princes of Gomorrah and saying: Why will you be struck any more, adding iniquity? I shudder all over and am flooded with tears. There is nothing more, he says, that can be added to your sins, nor can anything further be sought out for vengeance. Everything has been so brought upon you, while some new kind of vengeance was always being devised against you, that you have exhausted every kind of plague. There is no longer, then, a wound or a scar or a swollen sore: there are sores over the whole body and soundness nowhere. For it is not possible, he says, to apply a poultice, nor oil, nor bandages. But I pass over the threat that follows, lest perhaps I become more burdensome to you than the very affliction of the present plague.

17. Yet we must recognise the causes of our evils: why the farmlands have dried up, why the granaries are thrown into disorder, why the pastures have failed the flocks, why their beauty has been taken from the lands, and why the fields are not filled with plenty, but everywhere is mourning and grief. Nowhere are the valleys filled with grain, nor have the mountains dripped sweetness as for the just; but on the contrary there is devastation everywhere and overthrow everywhere, and everywhere [the lands] receive the curse of the mountains of Gilboa. We have become as at the beginning, before the earth brought forth every green herb. You have indeed visited your land, Lord, and made it drunk, but with a most evil visitation and with drunkenness from the wine of compunction. A cruel and horrid sight! All the hope of the year has remained to us in stubble alone, and scarcely anyone may find ears to gather, to offer firstfruits to the Lord. Perhaps the mice will store our harvests in the granaries; for no one will bind a sheaf. These are the riches of the impious, such is the crop of those who sow through injustice. So the prophets describe the curses of the ancients when they say: He will carry out much and bring in little; he will sow and not reap; he will plant a vineyard and not press wine; and where ten yoke of oxen labour, he will make one jar. Whence, then, this cause of evils, whence the occasion of devastation? Let us not wait to be rebuked by others; let us accuse ourselves, let us rebuke ourselves. The remedy of evil is the confession of error. I first, just as I proclaimed before to my people and fulfilled the work of a watchman and did not hide or keep silent about the sword that was coming, so as to save both my own soul and the souls of those who were willing to hear me, so now too I declare and set forth the contempt and negligence of my people, making their wounds my own, in case even in this way we may obtain something of the divine mercy and clemency.

18. So one of us has oppressed the poor man and unjustly seized part of his little field, or has overstepped boundaries, whether by stealth or by violence, and joined house to house and field to field so as to take away something of his neighbour's, and has made it his chief concern to have no neighbour, as if he were to dwell alone upon the earth. Another has defiled the land with usury and the multiplying of interest, gathering where he did not scatter and reaping where he did not sow, cultivating not the land but greed. Another, having gathered very plentiful crops and a most abundant vintage, offered firstfruits neither from the threshing-floors nor from the winepresses to God, who granted the abundance of crops, and proved at once ungrateful and foolish, that is, he neither gave thanks for what he had obtained nor was found dutiful for what he hoped for. Another has not pitied the widow and the orphan, nor broken his bread for the hungry — rather, he has not refreshed the hungry Christ, who is fed in each of the least ones —; and there is he who beyond hope stores so much in his granaries, or rather who has nowhere to store it, and pulls down some granaries and builds others to prepare for future crops, not knowing that perhaps before that they will demand his soul from him, and there he will render account of the things he received generously and shut up narrowly, having become the bad steward of a good God. Another has shut off the way of the humble and turned aside the just man unjustly; another has hated him who rebuked in the gates and has cursed the holy word; another has sacrificed to his net, which had enclosed much, and has kept the plunder of the poor in his houses, having become forgetful of God, or at any rate mindful of him wrongly, when he said: Blessed be the Lord, for we have become rich, and harboured the iniquitous thought that he had from God what he was seizing unjustly. For these things, then, the wrath of God has come upon us, sons of perdition. For these things heaven is shut, and it will be shut still much more, if we do not turn at least after the scourges and draw near to him who draws near to us.

19. What do we say to these things, we who store up grain and trade on other people's hunger, who watch for bad times so that it may go well with us, who look for another's grief to become our joy, who say: When will the month pass, so that we may pile up prices? When will the sabbath pass, so that we may open our storehouses? You who set out double measures and deceitful weights, and yourselves heap up against yourselves measures of punishments and torments, what do you say to these things, you who acknowledge no limit to possession, who worship gold and silver as a god, or rather adore them as Baal, who pursue every precious thing in gems and soft, delicate garments, and gather treasures for moths and thieves, puffed up by a multitude of slaves and a great number of horses and other animals, spread out over whole stretches of plains and ridges of mountains? Some things you possess, others you seize, and the rest you hope for, like that leech of Solomon which can in no way be filled, like the underworld and water and fire, you who seek another world for your possession, as though finding fault with the narrow spaces of possessions created for us by God. And what of those who sit on the lofty seats of the tribunals and, holding the power of judging, puffed up with haughty brow, give no thought at all that they too are to be judged by God, who is the true judge of all, so that they too might temper their power as toward fellow servants, knowing that they too need the clemency of God? And what about those who lounge on beds of ivory? Of them holy Amos fittingly made mention: who, he says, are anointed with the finest ointments and clap their hands to the sound of instruments, and have thought these fleeting things to be lasting, and have suffered nothing at the affliction of Joseph, that is, they have not pitied the fall of their neighbours. For they ought to have been kind and merciful toward those who had been chastised before them, and by mercy to call forth mercy. The pine ought to have wept because the cedar fell, and to have been amended by the amendment nearby and to correct their own evils from the evils of others, since they saw that they had obtained this benefit, that while others were scourged they themselves could obtain salvation, when it could certainly have happened that, they being scourged, others were amended.

20. Discourse on these things to the people together with us, O head venerable to me and most gentle, since much experience of long time is in you. Instruct the people and teach them to break their bread for the hungry, to bring the poor and the homeless into their house, to cover the naked, not to despise poor kinsfolk, and now above all, so that our good may not always come from abundance, but also from want. For God rejoices more in such a sacrifice than in those things which are offered from abundance. Become for us today a Moses or a Phinehas; stand for us before God and make him propitious again, so that the devastation may at last cease, whether through spiritual sacrifice or through prayers and supplications, only so that you may meet the wrath of the Lord and, standing in the middle, make what remains of the plague cease. God gladly embraces the grey hair of a father poured out in intercession for his sons. Make supplication for past evils, intercede for future ones; offer to God a people already purged by plagues and fear, already amended by the scourges of devastation; obtain for them bodily food, but before that the angelic food itself that comes down from heaven; reconcile God to men, rejoin heavenly things to earthly; call back to the earth the early and the late rains: the Lord will give a blessing and our land will give its fruit, this land which is below the daily [fruit], and our land the everlasting, which it first brought forth in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power for ages of ages. Amen.

IX. On the Arians.

1. Our discourse is to those who are clever in speech, and I shall begin from the scriptures. Behold, I am against you, he says, insolent one. For there are some with itching ears and tongue, and now indeed, as I see, also hand, who with profane novelties of words and with questions and objections of falsely so-called knowledge stir up battles of words to no profit. For so Paul names everything that is superfluous and over-curious in words, since he himself is the preacher and champion of the shortened word. These people, then, of whom our discourse is, and above all the Arians, if only, just as they have a tongue both fluent and vehement, they would likewise use words that are right and commendable, and would give themselves a little to the works of God's commandments too! Perhaps they would be less like sophists in words and would stir up fewer controversies about the simplicity of the scriptures.

2. For all of them, leaving all the other ways of piety, look and aim at this one thing: whether they can perhaps bind something fast in questions, or how they may undo things said simply and faithfully, as sometimes happens in an athletic contest, where in the sport of wrestling one strives not so much for the palm as for a display of holds and skill that wins the favour of the spectators. So these men too, hunting the applause of hearers, make the streets and public places resound with disputes, and every banquet and every festival, and even times of mourning, if they have entered, they fill entirely with questions and contests, so that the solemnity loses its festivity and joy, and mourning lacks consolation. And entering the gatherings of women too, to whom simplicity ought surely to be native and their companion from birth, with the importunate and rapid movements of their words they strip them of all modesty and the flower of shame. Since, then, these things are so, and this evil advances intolerably, and that great mystery of our religion is being reduced to a kind of trickery and an art of words, in this at least we ask that whoever has given himself over to the workshops of such disputes should comply with us: that they not receive with scorn what we are moved to by fatherly affection toward them, while we give an account of each of these matters, and that they restrain their tongue for a little, if indeed they can, and grant us only a hearing. For what loss, I ask you, will you suffer from this? Either we have spoken into the ears of hearers and our speech has found fruit, your salvation — since he who sows the word sows it in every heart, but it bears fruit only from soil that is rich and good — or, if our speech has brought forth nothing worthy to move you, you will go away despising us, taking from this even more material for contradicting us and despising what we assert. I do not want you, then, to be surprised if I seem to you to bring forward a surprising speech, one against both your custom and your law, you who promise either to know or to teach everything with a magnificent and lofty promise, not to say an intemperate and shameless one, lest perhaps you be grieved.

3. It is not for everyone, O most prudent men, to dispute about God; it is not for everyone to examine the divine nature. The language of sacred scripture is not so cheap as to lie open to the untaught crowd and to little men still crawling on the earth. I shall add this too, that these things are not to be brought forward always, nor all of them, nor to all, nor by all, but there is a when, and a to whom, and a how far. It is not, then, for everyone to raise such questions, but for those who have spent their talent and industry in the disciplines of contemplation and knowledge, and for those who know how, setting aside bodies and matter, to behold incorporeal and spiritual things; but above all it belongs to those who are already purified in soul and body, or at the least who are certainly being purified. For he who is less pure, how does he dare touch the pure? Since even weak eyes do not look on the rays of the sun with impunity. So we can perceive something of such things only if we keep leisure and quiet and hold ourselves back from all the enticements of bodily matter that disturb us from outside, if our mind stands firm without any sedition of desires and thoughts. But how do we mix holy and pure things with impure and filthy movements? It is as if someone were to mix sweet perfumes with the stench of mud and pour nectar on dung. First of all, then, we must be still and know God, and when we receive the time for judging justice, then we shall also judge what it is just to think about God. And to whom are these things to be brought forward or imparted? First to those who have turned the studies of their whole life to this, and from whom discourse about God is not required as just one thing among others, after the circus, after the theatres, after those songs too in which they have delighted, after the care of the belly and of what lies below the belly; by whom it is even counted as a kind of entertainment if a dispute about divine things is stirred up, so that they may take delight in the contest of controversies. And about what are we to dispute, and how far? About those things which it is possible to grasp, and as far as the strength and capacity of the hearer can receive, lest perhaps, just as excess of sound injures the hearing and abundance of food corrupts the distended stomach, so too the mind, receiving the food of the word beyond its measure, either collapse stunned or be tormented by being too distended. Look, then, if you please, at those who strive to lift burdens beyond their strength, or when the earth is pressed by excessive and immense rains, how harmful is whatever goes beyond measure. So it must be considered that someone weighed down by the burden of the word may, by that very excess, run the risk even of his common and natural understanding.

4. And I do not say this because one ought not always to remember God, lest perhaps those who are quick to twist simple statements into a perverse sense should rise up against us again from another side. One ought always to remember God, even more often than to breathe. And if it is possible to say or to do, nothing other than this should be done, since I too commend meditating on the law of the Lord day and night, as the scriptures teach, and at evening and at night and at noon to tell of and bless the Lord at all times and, as Moses says, lying in bed and rising up and walking on the way. And whatever else a man does, it is expedient always to keep God and the memory of God fixed in the heart. So I do not forbid having the memory of God always, but I do not advise disputing about God always and out of season. Indeed not even in this do I forbid what is pious, but what is out of season; I do not prohibit teaching, but I cut off immoderation. Or does not a surfeit and excess even of honey cause vomiting? And what is sweeter than honey? But there is a time for everything, as it seems to Solomon and to me. For a good thing becomes not good if it is not done well. Or is it not out of season to look for flowers in winter, and quite incongruous for a woman to wear men's ornaments or for a woman's necklace to be fitted on a man? It is absurd both to press geometry on a mourner and to spoil a banquet with weeping. All these things, then, require their own fitting time: and are we the only ones who do not recognise the fitness of times, we among whom above all fitness in all things ought to be kept?

5. By no means, I beg you, O friends and brothers — for I still call you brothers, although you are unwilling to keep anything brotherly toward us — let us not take counsel in this way about the greatest matters, nor, as hot and restless horses are wont to do, throw off our charioteer, that is, the fear of God, wantonly and impudently, and wander far from the fixed limits of the turning-posts; but rather let us philosophise within the lines marked out for us, and neither turn back again into Egypt nor be carried off to the Assyrians, nor sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land, that is, into every ear that is foreign and hostile to our religion. For they, when they have heard carefully and retained what is ours, at once strive to blow up huge fires from our sparks, which are swept up to heaven by hidden and pressing blasts and make for us those lofty Babylonian flames that lick round everything in their circuit. Since indeed they have no confidence in their own doctrines, they hunt in ours for anything they may find weak or fragile, not so much by its own nature as through the feebleness of the one asserting it, and then, as flies settle on wounds, so they settle on every error or fragile word of ours. But let us no longer be ignorant of ourselves, nor refuse to inquire what is fitting in such matters. Even if it is impossible for us to think as one with contention set aside, let it at least be right to ratify a common pact in this: that we not profane the holy mysteries in public, that we not handle holy things unholily, and that we not plunge what we have received through an ineffable sacrament into profane ears and polluted consciences, nor make more respectable those who worship images and venerate idols, who, serving shameful mysteries and fables, would more readily give up their blood for what they think mysteries than a word of them to those who have not been initiated into such things. But let us see whether, just as a man's robe, the laughter of his teeth and the gait of his feet show some signs of his honour from the very moderation and temperance of the man himself, so too the utterance of speech and the restraint of silence may give some sign of both our religion and our learning, since indeed among the other names and powers which it is lawful for men to apply to God, we also name him the Word. Now then, if our purpose is to contend, let at least our contention itself be lawful.

6. Why does the profane hearer hear of the birth of God, and his creation, and God from things non-existent, and the section, splitting and dissolution of the substance? Why do we call our accusers and enemies as judges of our words? Why do we hand over our swords to the enemy? How do you think they hear a word about such things, with what mind, with what sense — those who praise adulteries and consecrate the defilement of boys and every kind of vice, who can perceive and understand nothing at all beyond the body, who a little before set up for themselves those gods whom they had come to know from baseness and crimes? Will not such people understand all these things carnally, all things basely and ignorantly? Will they not judge our things as they judge their own, and with the same feeling and sense with which they take the generations of their gods and the begetting of sons, weigh ours too? When they utter words of this kind, do we not both laugh at them and attack them? And how shall we persuade them to accept what is ours, if they see contests stirred up again among ourselves about the same things? This is what this contention among us brings us, this is what a contest brings us waged for the Word in a way other than pleases the Word himself. We suffer in a way what madmen suffer, who set fire to their own houses with their own hands, or slaughter their sons, or drive away their parents, thinking them strangers.

7. Since, then, we have destroyed what is foreign to the religion of the Word of God, and cast the manifold legion into the herd of swine, which was also hurled into the deep, let us now look at what concerns ourselves. This, then, is what I think must first be considered: what is this great contention over words alone? What itch of the tongue is this, what great impatience? Why is it that, with our hands drawn back and bound, we bring forth the works and weapons of the tongue alone? The pursuit of charity ceases; that of chastity, virginity, mercy is either lacking or, if it exists in some, it is either rare or less vigorous. There is not so much care for psalm-singing, nor for vigils, nor for prayers, no zeal for weeping in supplications, nor for humbling the body by fasts, nor for ascending to God through intent prayer — we do not join what is worse to what is better, I mean clay to spirit; we do not practise the meditation of death in life; we are not kindled to master the vices, mindful of our heavenly kinship — nor to conquer rage or restrain anger, nor to cast down arrogance or drive away irrational sorrow, nor to bridle lust, nor to cut back intemperance of laughter, the wantonness of the eyes, intemperance of hearing, immoderation of speech, nor to blunt the vanity of thoughts, whether those the enemy suggests to us or those he takes from us, through which indeed, as Scripture says, he brings in death through the bodily senses as through windows. But on the contrary, we grant all these vices freedom to wander wherever they will and however we do not will, and we think we keep caution only in disputations and questions.

8. And indeed, O talkative dialectician, I will ask you some small thing; answer me, as he said who spoke to Job through the whirlwind and cloud. Are there not many mansions with God? I think you do not deny what is written. What then? Must all these be filled, or some filled and others not, so that they remain empty and seem to have been prepared in vain? I know you will grant that all are to be filled; for you will admit that nothing was made by God in vain. And this very thing we call a mansion, what do you think should be understood by it? Is it not the rest and glory which is laid up for the blessed? You will not grant it to be anything else, I think. If, then, this is certain, it follows that we inquire whether there is something that procures these mansions for each of us. Beyond doubt there must be. What, then, will it be that calls each one to the different mansions? Is it not the diversity of deeds and of purpose, according to the measure of each one's faith, spent in this light, which divine Scripture is also accustomed to call ways? What then? Must we travel by all these ways, or by some of them? If indeed it were possible, it would be blessed for one person to walk by all; if not, by as many as he can, or at least by some; if not even that, at least to walk rightly and faultlessly by one. If, then, you hear that there is one way and that it is narrow, what do you think is indicated? Is not the one way to be understood as the unity of the virtues? For virtue is one, even if it seems to be divided into many. And it is called narrow because of the labours, and because it is not readily accessible to many. What then, dearest one? If the division of many ways, and again the narrowing and gathering of the one, is such as we said above, through what ignorance or intemperance do we cram ourselves into these straits, so that, as if placed in utmost want, leaving all the ways which the word of God teaches us, we press on this one alone and confine ourselves in this one, which consists in debate and mere disputation of words, and which, as it seems to me, is sought not so much from zeal for wisdom and knowledge as from the vice of talkativeness? Does not the blessed apostle Paul rebuke you about these things, who, after listing the spiritual gifts, goes on and says: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? and so on.

9. Grant that you are someone lofty, and higher than the lofty, and ascend above the clouds, if you like, and behold invisible things and grasp ineffable things in speech; be taken up above Elijah, and above Moses see God face to face, if you can; be raised above Paul too to the heights of the third heaven: why do you want to fashion others too into saints in a day? Why do you make theologians in a moment of time, to discourse on the divine nature while they are still wholly ignorant of their own life, so that you think they have received a teaching breathed in by you rather than worked out by toil, and why do you hold very many assemblies with the words of the unskilled? Why do you bind the weak in spiders' webs and draw them in as if about to bestow some wisdom on them? Why do you stir up a swarm of wasps against the faith? Why does dialectic believe it adorns religion, when rather religion is defiled through dialectic? That fabled Battle of the Giants is in a way renewed for us now, while war is waged against God on earth; and while every word is uttered with a question, the tongue becomes a warrior, words are javelins, speech is a sword, the fight goes on all day without any end, and at times each side is laid low by mutual wounds. But if the love of this war is so great, if the zeal for contest so great, if it pleases to win the triumphs of dialectical battle, let us, I beg, desist from civil wars: let us take up external and hostile wars.

10. Let us fight against the Pythagorean silences and destroy the Orphic beans. Let us refute that presumptuous saying of the Pythagoreans about their master: "He himself said"; let us confute Plato's ideas and the opinion about the soul being poured across into various kinds of bodies, which they call *metensomatosis* [re-embodiment], and certain cycles of our souls through various lives, and recollections, and other things like these. Let us attack Epicurus, with his god who does not perceive and his denial of providence; let us speak against his atoms and his pleasure, which, against the dignity of philosophy, he declares to be the highest good, and let us overthrow them. Let us confute Aristotle's narrow opinion about providence, and his faithless art of words, and the reasonings he put forward about the soul, and his doctrines, human rather than divine. Let us bring down the lofty brow of the Stoics, and the vile, gluttonous practice of the Cynics from the crossroads. Let us overthrow the vanity, full of ridiculous fables, of those who assert multitudes of gods, who offer sacrifices to images, who pour libations to demons evil and good. Let us be roused against those who marvel at divinations, auspices, auguries, invocations of demons and other similar monstrosities. Let us toil against those who weigh their lives by the motions or courses of the stars, who assign their own negligence and sloth to fate and the stars, and ascribe the incomprehensible ordering of divine providence to the chances of a fortune that is, as they say, blind and playful. But if these things seem to you unworthy and small, to hurl the darts of your disputations against, as things often refuted by many and frequently crushed, and it pleases you more to exercise yourself on our own and proper matters, I will prepare for you open fields of contest even in these. Dispute about the world or worlds, about matter; dispute about the soul, about rational natures, about the glory of the resurrection, about the judgement, about recompense, about the sufferings of Christ. For on these matters it will not be useless to grasp what is true, and to err in some point carries no danger from God. And in this we shall receive grace, now indeed small, according to our strength, but afterwards more perfect, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power for ages of ages. Amen.
